speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSAL TO AMEND IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could have the indulgence of the house to make a brief statement about the bill to amend the Defence Production Act.
After consulting the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as to the best way to ensure effective parliamentary control over the administration of the act, I wish to announce that when the bill is in committee I will propose the addition of a third section to provide that orders made under the Defence Production Act, either by the governor in council or by the minister, shall, in addition to the normal publication in the Canada Gazette, be laid upon the table of both houses of parliament at the earliest possible moment after they are made, and that a notice of motion signed by ten members praying for the repeal or amendment of any such order if given within seven days of the tabling of the order in either house shall be debated at the first convenient opportunity within the next four sitting days.
The government has been able to think of no more effective way of ensuring prompt parliamentary control of the exercise of the powers under this act and we hope this proposal will commend itself to all sections of the house.

Has the Prime Minister, since speaking a year or so ago at Calgary, Alberta, on the subject, given any direction or order to any department of government to change the expression or term "Riel rebellion" to "Riel uprising", in official documents?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be permitted to answer this question orally. The answer is "no". There is only one incident to which the question refers and it is not accurately described in the question. The question is:
Has the Prime Minister, since speaking a year or so ago at Calgary, Alberta, on the subject, given any direction or order to any department of government to change the expression or term "Riel rebellion" to "Riel uprising", in official documents?
As I said, there was only the one incident. It was not a year ago; it was four years ago. It was not at Calgary, Alberta; it was at Battleford, Saskatchewan. It was not in the course of a public address; it was in the course of a conversation with the supervisor of the fort at Battleford. It was prompted by reports which I had, during my visit to that part of Saskatchewan, of difficulties arising out of the defacing of the inscription on the monument at Batoche; the incident received a lot of publicity at the time. When I got back to Ottawa I found that this publicity had come to the notice of the then minister of resources and development and had been referred by him to the historic sites and monuments board for consideration at their next meeting. So I did nothing more about it.

The house resumed, from Thursday, June 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe, Port Arthur (for Mr. St. Laurent) for the

second reading of Bill No. 256, to amend the Defence Production Act.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a few moments ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a statement concerning a proposal on the government's part with regard to this act and orders made under it. Any comment on that particular proposal I shall leave to others because, without seeing it and examining it closely, I might form an impression that some great concession has been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. At the moment I think it does not go beyond what is already open to the members of this house on any occasion. Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last, close to the hour of adjournment, I was dealing with this subject and I pointed out that our opposition to the bill was not factious at all but was based on sound ground, namely that extraordinary powers such as those which are contained in the act-and which are admitted by the minister to be extraordinary-should not be made permanent. I indicated the points of agreement and the points of difference. I showed that in March, just three months ago, we came close to reaching a compromise and that, after debate at the resolution stage, we were left with the impression that the bill would be altered in such a way as to make it acceptable to all parties in this house. Then to our surprise, of course, it was brought in a little while ago without any alteration.
In the course of the debate various members on the other side of the house and elsewhere have said that we in the opposition have made no suggestion with regard to changing the act but that we had just been criticizing it. I would say that they have not been following the debate very closely because several good suggestions have been made; and if any one of those suggestions had been adopted by the government this debate would soon be brought to an end.
For example, the suggestion was made that certain sections in the act be amended in such a way that some of the extraordinary powers would terminate at a specified time. The second suggestion made was that the expiry date be advanced by one to three years. The third suggestion was that the act be split so that the department would be made permanent-something on which there is general agreement-and that the rest of the act would terminate unless periodically renewed by parliament.
I think the best solution to this problem is to make two acts instead of one. I have examined the statutes in order to see how 50433-296J
Defence Production Act the other departments are set up. While I have not made an exhaustive survey, I find that twelve of the other departments are set up by short acts running from two to three pages. The Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) is also the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In chapter 78 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, I find that department to be set up by a short act running just over one page. In that short act there are several sections doing just the normal things such as declaring that there shall be a department; appointing a minister; making the Minister of Trade and Commerce a member of the privy council; saying that he has management of the department; giving the governor in council authority to appoint a deputy minister and such other officers, clerks and employees as are necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the department. Then section 5 deals with the duties of the minister; section 6 puts the Canada Grain Act under his management; and section 7 says that he shall present an annual report to parliament. Why could not that be done with this particular department?
Why could there not be a separate act setting up the Department of Defence Production, making it permanent and giving the minister the opportunity of retaining experienced employees, and then a second act outlining the methods of defence procurement and all the other things that are contained in the present act? Alternatively, if that is not accepted, the present act could be divided into distinct parts. The part dealing with the organization of the department could be made permanent and such other parts as seem fit could be made of short duration. That and the other things I have mentioned have been concrete suggestions advanced by the opposition, and when the opportunity comes in the committee stage it is possible that amendments may be used to indicate that very clearly.
The whole trouble facing us, Mr. Speaker, is that there is a fundamental difference between those of us in Her Majesty's loyal opposition and the minister. The minister set out his point of view last week. He said that we had been suggesting that the traditional methods of parliamentary procedure and parliamentary responsibility were being interfered with, that there was a denial of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law, and he stated that he was only a layman in this field. That struck me as being an astonishing statement. Granted that on the face of it it was very modest and unassuming, but I thought it was peculiar that a senior member of the house, after 20 years

Defence Production Act in parliament and 20 years as a cabinet minister, would say that he was only a layman with regard to the usages and customs of parliament, the duties and responsibilities of members of this chamber, and the responsibility of the cabinet and individual ministers to parliament.
I think it is incumbent upon the senior members of the house to be the foremost to defend the parliamentary system, to exercise moderation with respect to any suggested changes and to restrain newcomers to the house when they appear to be impatient with the parliamentary system. I regret to say that the minister has unfortunately gained the reputation of being rather impatient with the parliamentary system. He has appeared to prefer to do things quickly rather than by the slower methods of parliament. He has gained a great reputation as a cutter of red tape, but he has no red tape to cut in legislation such as this because he has made perfectly sure there are no strings attached whatever.
It is because of his attitude that there appears to be a fundamental difference dividing us on this occasion. Actually he is attempting to reverse the process. Normally ministers come to parliament and ask for extension of their powers or for special powers for special purposes and parliament examines the situation, makes the grant of power and withdraws it when the crisis has subsided. If the legislation is to be continued, as the minister desires, and is made permanent with all the powers contained therein, parliament will be in the position of having to go to the minister and beg him to surrender his powers. In that regard he said the other day that he will decide if and when the act shall be liquidated and not parliament, although in March the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said that parliament would decide. I suggest, therefore, that an attempt is being made to reverse the normal processes of parliamentary procedure.
Now, I have pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has declared himself to be a layman with regard to matters that concern parliament. After 20 years he has not learned, as he implied, very much about the parliamentary system. Certainly, he has not learned to admire it. Although he is very modest and unassuming in that statement, he was far from modest and unassuming when he declared that after 20 years in this parliament, and his long term of service as the minister in charge of the department, he felt, and these are his words as recorded on page 4512 of Hansard for June 7, 1955:
... I think I can claim to have more experience in defence purchasing than any other man now living.

Those are not the words of a layman, nor the words of one who is modest and unassuming. Yet I would suggest that he has become an acknowledged authority in defence purchasing by virtue of the position conferred upon him by successive prime ministers and the authority granted to him by parliament.
There is nothing I am saying in connection with this act which would indicate for one minute that this party is opposed to proceeding rapidly with the defence build-up that is necessary under the circumstances. My own opinion is that we should get on with the job, and get on with it rapidly. The radar warning screens must be completed as rapidly as possible up north or they may be obsolete by the time they are completed. Aeroplanes must continue to come off the assembly line as quickly as possible because they become obsolete so quickly. Guided missiles are required at the earliest possible date. Consequently, I say, get on with the job.
If there is a real emergency within the proper definition of that term I gave to the house the other day, then I say we should be informed and all the steps should be taken that are necessary to meet that emergency, including a general organization of the country so that it can present a united effort in time of peril. It means also the imposition of controls and giving full power to the cabinet, as was done in wartime. Canada will respond as Canada has always responded. But if the minister is not prepared to do that, if the situation is not that serious, then I say to him, let the parliamentary system continue in full force and effect; let the rule of law be honoured in the land. Let the minister be content with the restraints that we are suggesting in point of time regarding the extraordinary powers he desires. Let him be content with some of the inconvenience and the slowness of the parliamentary system. Let him effect a compromise.
During the last 50 years in the modern world we have observed experiments with all the forms of government that mankind has devised in centuries. We have seen absolute monarchies, and we have seen them destroyed. We have seen dictators rise and fall. We have experienced war and revolution. We have observed democracies destroyed from within. We have seen oligarchies set up. There is no known form of government that has not been tried within the last 50 years, and we still think our democratic system and our parliamentary form of government is better than any other method of governing mankind that has been devised. We think it

protects the rights of the individual and provides freedom within the law. It is on that basis, then, that I suggest we should be vigilant to maintain our system, and we are on sound ground when we object to any encroachment on this system of government which has proven its worth over the years. We are quite prepared to admit that it has faults and weaknesses, but what is the alternative? I do not find the alternative, as the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Phil-pott) does, in the "great man" theory of government, as he came very close to doing the other day when he attempted, in what I think was fulsome flattery, to indicate to this house that the present Minister of Defence Production was the architect of victory in the last war. So far as Canada is concerned, I thought it was the co-operative effort of millions of Canadians that achieved that victory.
I believe in giving credit where credit is due. I think that the minister is one of the ablest men in Canada. I have respect for his ability and experience. I like men of action; I like men of decision; and the minister has admirable qualities. I respect him for them. I think he should similarly respect us for our position when we say and proclaim that the parliamentary system is being endangered by this act which he wishes to make permanent.
He suggests that he is not fully informed with regard to the parliamentary system as it has been devised, and we think that he is now trying to put shackles and restraints on the very institution that made it possible for him to achieve greatness. It was as a result of this institution and his position here that he achieved a position of commanding importance in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate we are dealing with questions which are obviously of the utmost importance not only to this house but to the whole of Canada. It is regrettable, Mr. Speaker, that on matters as important as this there is such confusion evident in the speeches of the members of the official opposition and of the Social Credit group. It appears evident that many of these hon. members are either unwilling or unable to recognize the realities of the situation with which we are confronted.
The subject matter of our discussion is plainly and simply the defence of Canada. The thing that is at stake is the ability of this country to provide the weapons, the materials, the projects and all the panoply of defence requirements that are needed by modern defence services to provide these not only for ourselves but in co-operation with our allies for the necessary defence of this continent, and to provide certain materials of war for our allies on other continents.
No member opposite has suggested that this is not an important task. But, Mr. Speaker, they have made the mistake of attempting to suggest that in trying to provide for the proper discharge of our responsibilities in this regard we are in some way subverting parliament and violating the rule of law.
I say to hon. members opposite, this is a completely mistaken view. They are misled if they believe that what is proposed here constitutes a threat to things that we on this side of the house believe in, support and have at heart just as much as have they or anybody else in this country. The confusion and the inconsistencies that are apparent in the hon. member's speech are almost too numerous to mention, and I shall deal only with several that I think are of particular importance.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), who has just taken his seat, gave us a perfect example just before he sat down. It is beyond me how he and other hon. members can in one breath express the greatest confidence in the Minister of Defence Production and refer to his tremendous record of achievement in this country, then in the very next breath attack the same minister and express the greatest concern about his powers, saying that he is an autocrat, that he is moved only by a lust and a desire for power.

Defence Production Act The first description that the hon. members are good enough to give of the minister is correct, and is proved by history. Their second contention is incorrect, and it is disproved by the same history. They cannot have it both ways. The minister has either done an outstanding job for this country in shouldering the very heavy responsibilities that have been placed upon him, or he is, as they suggest, a dangerous autocrat who is trying either to socialize or to centralize this country. Hon. members can juggle these two inconsistent and mutually contradictory statements as much as they like in efforts to bolster up their arguments in this debate, but when one listens to their speeches and reads them it becomes more than obvious that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Phil-pott) was correct the other night when he said that what is going on here is opposition for opposition's sake and that we are in fact seeing a filibuster on that basis.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the real disagreement between those who support this bill and those who oppose it can be reduced to a very small compass, and in fact can be stated in two quite simple questions. The first is: what is the real nature and extent of the powers contained in the Defence Production Act? The second is, are these powers reasonably necessary in the present circumstances? If the answer to the latter question is yes, can we at this time foresee a definite time in the future when these powers will no longer be required?
First of all let us look at the Defence Production Act, particularly in the light of certain charges that have been made with respect to it and the powers which it contains. The first speaker in this debate for the official opposition was the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and he certainly established himself as an all-time long distance champion in this session and perhaps in many others.

He was the first to read a number of quotations both relevant and irrelevant, and his colleagues have followed his example so that we have seen them delving further and further into both literature and doggerel in order to take up the time of the house. The hon. member for Eglinton read into the record a number of sections of the Defence Production Act. He read some of them in whole and some in part. I presume that he disapproves of those which he read into the record as examples of improper powers, and that he equally disapproves of all that he read. Presumably he approves of the powers which he did not

read into the record or disapproves of them less than he does of those which he selected. He certainly gave no contrary indication.
The hon. member commenced by reading section 15 of the act and his words in that respect appear on page 4519 of Hansard of June 7. I invite hon. members to read carefully this section, as the hon. member for Eglinton invited them to do. What is this section?
It is a detailed and clearly worded section which sets out in specific terms certain powers for the carrying out of defence procurement. Surely there must be a section of this nature in any defence production act. By this section parliament not only grants powers but clearly sets limitations to those powers. By the very fact that parliament enacts a section of this kind it asserts its authority to grant these powers and to oversee them. What is so unusual and improper about the words from section 15 which the hon. member read into the record? I submit that there is nothing unusual or improper except that the powers are admittedly wide powers; but that is dictated by the importance and the complexity of the task set for the department and for the minister, and for no other reason.
Then the hon. member referred in passing to section 16, and then went on-still at page 4519-to read section 17. I once again invite hon. members to read what the hon. member put on the record, but to read the whole section and not just the sections which he placed on Hansard. Does the hon. member for Eglinton want section 17 of the act eliminated? I doubt very much that he does, and he certainly did not take the responsibility of saying so. By this section we in parliament lay down strict rules governing the manner in which the department and the minister and the government may exercise the powers given them elsewhere in the act. It gives the power to enter into contracts, but only in certain specific ways and always subject to the requirements of the act. If the hon. member for Eglinton and other hon. members are arguing that this section should be removed, it simply means that they want to remove these restrictions on the manner in which the minister and the department can carry out their duties and responsibilities.
The hon. member appeared to be particularly concerned with subsection (e) of this section and he invited hon. members to pay particular attention to that subsection. I invite the hon. member and his colleagues to pay particular attention to some other statutes. If the hon. member will read section 37 of the Public Works Act, chapter 228 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, he will

find there a subsection very similar in terms to subsection (e) of section 17 of the Defence Production Act. It provides that in certain specific circumstances contracts may be entered into and the approval of the governor in council secured later by notice. That is the provision in that act and I have never heard hon. members opposite claim that the Public Works Act gives sweeping or arbitrary or improper powers to the minister or to the government.
The hon. member then went on to quote parts of section 24, parts of section 27, section 28, section 30, section 31 and section 32, and never took the responsibility of indicating whether he objected to the whole of those sections, to part of them or just what specific objection he had. No wonder the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who followed the hon. member in the debate, had reason to remark that after 101 minutes the hon. member had still not made clear his position or the position of his party.
I must say that after listening to the hon. member for Eglinton I got the impression that he started out reading these sections and then after he completed reading them he realized that having heard them read out aloud he did not feel that they went quite so far or were quite as objectionable as apparently he had imagined they were when he had been thinking things over in the quiet of his own office. Then he simply went on to the next section in the hope that he would find something better there. What is quite apparent from a reading of the portions of these sections which the hon. member did not put on the record is that he omitted to read all the provisions of these sections which provided limitations on the powers and authority given under those sections and limiting their use strictly to securing the basic purposes of the legislation.
I should like now to turn to the speech made by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). During that speech we heard all the familiar phrases and slogans to which we have become so accustomed in this house, generalized complaints and protests which sound fine but which when examined are found to have very little relation to the facts. I think it is a great pity that important and fundamental concepts of our constitution and form of government, such as the rule of law, tend in the mouth of the hon. member for Prince Albert to become mere meaningless catch phrases which are applied holus-bolus to any problem that comes up.
The hon. member attacked the Defence Production Act mainly on the ground that it
Defence Production Act violates the rule of law by denying to the subject recourse to the courts in connection with actions taken by the department and the minister under the act. We had a ringing and resounding speech from him on this subject. The only thing wrong with what the hon. member had to say was that there simply was no foundation in fact. I assure every hon. member in this house that there will not be found in the Defence Production Act a word, a phrase or a section that in any way limits or restricts the right of the subject to recourse to the courts if he feels aggrieved or suffers damage by any action taken by the minister, by the governor in council or by the department under this act. There is one exception to what I have said, and that is section 37. Section 37 restricts the personal liability of a controller or an investigator appointed under the act for anything done in good faith and within his powers under the act, but that same section specifically saves and excepts the right of the subject to recourse against the crown if there is any reason for recourse.
The hon. member said in definite terms that this act puts the minister and the government above the courts. That statement is completely without foundation in the act itself. As a matter of fact, the exact opposite is true. Section 22, for example, provides a special procedure whereby a person who disagrees with an order made under certain sections of the act can simply give notice in the exchequer court of appeal against the order and immediately there is a stay of all proceedings under that order, and the court assumes jurisdiction and deals with the matter without the necessity of the person aggrieved even commencing an action against the crown. The section gives specifically to the court the jurisdiction to vary or change in any way that it may deem just the order made by the minister.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, that is a special procedure to assist the subject in getting before the exchequer court without the necessity of starting an action and going through the whole rigmarole of an action, but under any other section of the act anybody who is aggrieved has full right to proceed by any of the normal procedures of getting before the court and getting a judgment on his case. This, Mr. Speaker, I submit, is not

Defence Production Act consistent with the contention that there is a denial of the right to appeal to the courts.
Fortunately, I have the courts on my side in this, because there was a very similar section in the munitions and supply act. An appeal was launched against several orders of the minister under that act and was heard by the exchequer court. There were three cases heard all together. One was Mulhol-land v. the Crown, 1952, Exchequer Court Reports, page 233. While I do not wish to follow the example of hon. members opposite in wearying the house with quotations, I should like to place on the record a brief quotation from the judgment of Cameron, J. in that case. He says this:
At first sight the powers conferred on the minister would seem to be somewhat arbitrary, but it is to be noted that section 13	(2) (re-enacted
1945 (Can.), c. 16, s. 11(1)) requires any person entering into a supply contract to keep detailed records and accounts of the cost of carrying out the contract and to make them available to the minister's representative. It may be assumed, therefore, that if the subsection were complied with, an appellant would have no great difficulty in presenting such evidence as would enable the court to properly review the minister's order and direction.
Where is there any suggestion that the court lacks any jurisdiction to properly review the minister's order or direction? Where is there any suggestion that the court felt that there was any denial of the right of the subject to appeal to that court? The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his colleagues are well aware that any attempt by legislation to exclude review by the courts of any action done under a statute must be expressed in explicit and clear language that the courts themselves with reluctance and hesitation find constitutes a clear expression of the will of parliament that such recourse be excluded.
It is understandable that the courts review any section of that kind with the greatest care. The hon. member knows, and all his colleagues know, that to achieve such an end by legislation the language has to be explicit and very carefully drawn. For example, you will have to use words such as this, and I quote as an example the following:
or render the commission, its servants or agents, or any municipal corporation or municipal commission, its or their servants or agents liable in any action at law or other legal proceedings for damages or otherwise.
The hon. member and his colleagues will recognize that there is a clear attempt, and a sweeping attempt, to remove certain matters from the jurisdiction of the courts, and hence a violation of the rule of law. The words are, "render" these people "liable in any action at law or other legal proceedings for damages or otherwise". The hon. members

cannot find any words of this nature in the Defence Production Act. Nor can they find any words that might possibly be interpreted as having the effect or the intention of excluding the jurisdiction of the courts in any way whatsoever, with the sole exception of section 37, to which I have already referred.
The hon. member for Prince Albert and his colleagues, if they are so interested in violations of the rule of law, might well be advised to take advantage of expert advice and opinion on these matters from sources which are very close at hand to them and which I believe they will recognize as worth while. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because the words I quoted as an example of a violation of the rule of law are taken from subsection 5 of section 71 of chapter 281 of the revised statutes of Ontario, the power commission act. These very words were inserted into that act by chapter 79 of the acts of 1947 when the hon. Leader of the Opposition was premier of the province of Ontario, and I understand that he personally introduced this amending bill into the legislature and piloted it through. If the hon. members want an example of a violation of the rule of law, there is a perfect and outstanding one for them to study. The result of all this is that the position of the hon. member for Prince Albert is untenable. He based his whole case on violations of the rule of law, and he is on a completely false premise.
This is largely true of a number of others who have spoken in the debate, such as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) and others. It is admitted that the powers in the Defence Production Act are wide, but it is submitted that they are necessary. They are subject to full and complete review in the courts and they are subject to full and complete review by parliament. Every action authorized by the act must be carried out strictly in accordance with the statute and the rules that parliament itself has laid down in the statute.
I come now to the equally important question of the need, in the present circumstances, for legislation of this kind. I am sure that we all envy the naive confidence of the hon. member for Calgary North and other members of the official opposition who have expressed such great delight and satisfaction with regard to the improvement in the international situation.

That fact, Mr. Speaker, raises problems not only for us but for our allies. There is a very prominent civil servant in the government employ today, one who is known to many hon. members in this house. As a young man he came to the attention of the minister of a certain department who interviewed him and wanted him to enter the government service. He was interviewed by the then prime minister, who asked him to come into the government service. But parliament was not in session and there had been no parliamentary appropriation made for that particular position the young man was to occupy. The minister and the prime minister told him regretfully that they could not take him into government service because parliament had not voted an appropriation for the salary for that position. However, a junior stenographer had left the service and they said that if the young man would accept an appointment as a junior stenographer he could be carried in that category until parliament met and voted an appropriation for his salary. The young man agreed to come in and later on parliament authorized his appointment.
This illustrates the strictness of parliamentary control within the lifetime of many people who are in this chamber. I am not saying it should be as strict today, with all the tremendous ramifications of government, but certainly we have gone a long way from that within the last few years.
We are asked now to go even further. I summarize it in this way, and say that parliament is asked to delegate tremendous powers to a minister and the minister in turn, under the act, can delegate those powers to a nominee of his who does not sit in this house or whose name may never be known to us. If we ask for the name we may be told it is not in the public interest to divulge the information. These nominees will be exercising functions which, constitutionally and traditionally, have only been exercised by parliament. There is no time limit on it. Once handed over, it is done once and for all. I say in bon mot that if parliament does that it may as well pull the blind, put out the cat and go to bed because there is very little left for it to do.
We are not arguing today about the extent of the powers, although I think those could be questioned and should be questioned in detail in committee. I feel those powers should be restricted in many ways. But the main gravamen of the offence, as I see it, is that parliament itself is delegating these powers and delegating them permanently. It will then be at the whim of the minister, as, if and when they will ever be returned to us.

I would be left, as I said earlier, with no remedy against the contractor but with some possible right of recovery from the crown. This applies to me as an individual, and it applies to municipalities. By order of the minister or some unknown nominee of his, people can be ordered, shall we say, from a county home and that building taken over. The same thing happens if a person is working for a province, even under statutory authority. One could go on and on giving simple little illustrations of what these powers mean. We say that, in the first place, they are too wide and in the second place, they should only be delegated for a reasonable time.
Now, if we were in the midst of a great crisis such as sometime might threaten us in this country, or as threatened Britain on the eve of the invasion, then certainly no one would question the delegation of powers. But we are not living in the horse and buggy age. We hope this is not the last session of parliament for a decade. Parliament can be summoned very quickly as we proved not many years ago. We have the war powers act in the background which always comes in automatically in the case of emergency.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition said none of you fellows believed in that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition will undoubtedly answer for himself. At the moment, I am dealing with this subject as I see it. Despite the protestations of the parliamentary assistant, I say there is not a scintilla of evidence at the moment that we are in any such crisis as requires even the operation of the bill to the extent in which it is drafted, let alone that permanent life be given to it. The hon. member for Halifax referred to the construction of the radar lines of the north, and the necessity for their erection. He cited that as justification for the passage of this bill by parliament. These matters, of course, are on the restricted list. The parliamentary assistant undoubtedly knows far more about them than we do. Possibly they are being proceeded with so

tardily that he is right in saying we shall need this bill some time in the future for their completion.
One would have thought from reading the press, and some of the guarded announcements that have been made, that these lines were fairly well along in the course of construction. This bill does not become operative until after July, 1956, because the present Defence Production Act does not expire until that date. If this bill is necessary for the construction of the radar lines in the north 14 or 15 months from now, then I believe it is a rather weak argument for the enactment of it. The minister says, and of course he was backed up by the parliamentary assistant this morning, that the situation is very bad. We know we are living in a state of tension. No one minimizes the dangers which confront us. Our point is, sir, that at least those tensions, so far as one can see, have not increased during the past few months and that we shall probably be living in a state of tension for many years to come. We should not, therefore, at one fell swoop, pass over all these powers to a minister for years, perhaps for a decade, and perhaps for much longer than that.
I do suggest in all seriousness that there is a lessening of tension. Even the extract which my hon. friend read from the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will bear that out.
I noticed an editorial yesterday-not that editorials are necessarily accepted as any foundation on which public policy should be established-I noticed an editorial in the New York Times of yesterday, the Sunday edition, which carries some weight generally. It speaks about winter passing and spring coming. It said that there was a lessening of tension. If things are so tense that we need to pass this bill at once, I rather question the judgment of a government that would permit or participate, or whatever they may have done, in the retirement of a chief of staff of wide experience and training in this moment of great crisis. It does not seem to be consistent, and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Defence Production spoke about consistency. We have of course the argument of fear psychology, which is used everywhere. It is said that the Russians have the bombs, and they may drop them, and therefore we must pass this bill.
There are some people, Mr. Speaker, who profess to be military authorities. Hanson Baldwin, for instance, says that now that the Russians have the bomb it has diminished tension, because you reach the stage where
Defence Production Act neither side would engage in a thermonuclear war. Therefore, at the moment we are back again to warfare with conventional weapons.
I am saying the minister has made no case whatsoever for increased tension which would require the passage of these clauses at this time, and certainly not on a permanent basis. Originally, the bill had a five-year limitation in it. I say no one can argue that today the times are more tense than they were in 1951. I am not going to repeat what others have said about tension at that time, about the experiences of the Korean war, the background of the United Nations' action, the background of the Berlin airlift and all this feeling of tension and crisis which was in the air in those days, the feeling of tension which produced this act. It had a five-year limitation. May I also refer to the tension which produced the emergency powers bill, which called on the government to come back year after year to get it extended.
Are we being unreasonable, Mr. Speaker, when we suggest that the minister should come back to parliament and ask for extensions and justify them from time to time, but not the creation of the department itself, and not all of the standard powers which may be required by the minister, the necessity for which we admit readily and unanimously. With respect to extraordinary powers which go farther than that, and which parliament can accept in times of emergency, we say simply that the minister must justify the continuance of those powers by parliament, and we are asking that he do so from time to time. That was the basis on which we reached a sort of agreement on the resolution stage.
Some of us were here that afternoon and that night, and we remember the huddle that went on. The Prime Minister was here; the Minister of Defence Production was here. I think that the Minister of Finance came in just at that time. Proceedings in the house stopped for two or three minutes while this whispered consultation went on. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) was urging a division. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) suggested that we wait until the result of the huddle, and then we got it. There was no guarantee; there was no commitment, except that if we would pass the resolution at that stage the government would give serious consideration to our proposal of a time limit to this legislation. No one believed that if the house leader made a statement such as that in the presence of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production it

Defence Production Act could not be carried out by the government, if a recommendation such as that were made.
I do not believe it was a parliamentary trick, Mr. Speaker. I do not think it was done to get us to pass the resolution that night and so they could say: Well, we fooled the opposition; we will go on to the next stage. I think they meant it. Certainly, the Liberal members who heard it thought they meant it, because I remember the comments in the corridors that night, as follows: Well, it is a sensible arrangement; it is a happy compromise. That was the unanimous opinion on all sides of the house, from just as many members supporting the Minister of Defence Production as on the opposition side, and I think 90 per cent of them feel the same way today.
Why the change? The hon. member for Halifax worries about criticism of an individual minister. You know sometimes one wonders whether they are not justified. Is it possible that someone said afterwards: Well, you know, that gives the opposition too much credit, because the papers in Canada came out the next day with editorials and headlines to the effect that the compromise was a satisfactory, a necessary and a proper one, and some of the opposition parties did get a little credit for it. It is possible that someone on the government side resented that and said: Oh, we have to look out; we do not want to give them any credit for it. Is it possible that on second thoughts, in the grey hours of the morning, someone believed that this was going to limit his powers too much, and said: We cannot agree to it; we cannot agree to any change. Is that why the change was made? I should like the Prime Minister, who took part in that huddle that night, to tell us why the government did not carry it out. I am not basing this on the fact that the Prime Minister's name was attached to the resolution. What I am saying is that he participated in that discussion and he owes the house an explanation as to why the government could not accept the suggestion.
The minister referred to the Department of Justice and suggested that the Department of Justice would find it difficult to draft such an amendment. If the Department of Justice would have any difficulty in that respect, and I am sure it would not, there are half a dozen lawyers on this side of the house and a dozen on the other side of the house, including the hon. member for Halifax, any one of whom could produce the necessary amendment in 15 minutes to carry out that suggestion, which was virtually agreed to that night. I do suggest if it had been accepted we would not find ourselves in the position in which we are here today.

All we are asking for, all that we want, is that the minister come to parliament instead of parliament having to go to the minister, with its hat in its hand, saying: Please, Mr. Minister, do you not think the time has come when you should amend or repeal some of these provisions? In other words, we want the minister to be responsible to parliament and not parliament to be responsible to the minister. That is the position in which we find ourselves, that is the position which we are fighting and we shall continue to fight.
The hon. member for Halifax says that we are talking for the sake of talking. Does he think that anyone enjoys standing up and prolonging this debate at this stage of the session? Some of us of necessity have to go home and earn a living. All of us want to get away, and none of us is taking any pleasure out of this. But we are sent here to do a job, and certainly we have some responsibility.
A man who has been around this place a long while, a cynic-I think he is a cynic; at least he is for my money-said to me on Saturday night: "George, don't waste your time talking about principles because that day is past. The people of Canada are not interested in principles any longer." I do not believe that, Mr. Speaker; I hope he is wrong. We, at least, are interested in principle and in trying to conserve the principle of parliamentary responsibility and parliamentary government, and that is all we are asking for.
Again, without indulging in personal attacks whatsoever, because I never do that, let me refer to what the minister said when he was asked about repeal or an amendment to this clause. I believe the quotation was changed, but we have it in Hansard at page 4542:
I do not propose to be told now-
I do not know whether the word "now" was put in then or later.
-by any hon. member just when X will liquidate it.
That is not the attitude the minister should take toward parliament when it is dealing with this legislation or amendments to it.
We are told that we have the estimates. The other day the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said that we have the estimates and that is parliamentary control. It is true to some extent that it is parliamentary control. It is true that it does give one a chance to ask questions; it gives one a chance to criticize and debate to a certain extent. But has anyone ever seen any effective check put upon the actions of a minister by a debate on the estimates? The most that you can do is to move a reduction

in the amount. Has that ever been done, or when it has been done has it ever carried in this house?
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has suggested that this proves that we are a democracy because we are debating it now. He asks, "What more do you want?" We know we are a democracy now; no one denies that. We want to be able to debate it five years from now or three years from now, to be able to debate not the principle of whether it has been carried on but the principle of whether it should be extended. That is why I say that this is the only way in which parliament can exercise control, by making it necessary to have these powers reviewed from time to time.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in an effort to justify their position said that this bill is necessary so that the government can control the wicked and rapacious corporations, these tremendous corporations which are in control of affairs. They contend that the only way in which the poor, little, helpless Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) would be able to deal with these horrible creatures would be to have these powers in this bill. I really weep when I hear that. I wept the other day when I saw what happened to the common man when the Ford Motor Company rammed down the throats of the members of the union a participation in the earnings of the corporation. They rammed down their throats what you might say was a guaranteed annual wage. Is it not terrible what this big corporation did? They just took those poor employees and choked them all and gave them a whole lot of things which undoubtedly they did not want to take; just forced them on them. I must say that that argument in justification of this bill was the most logical and sensible one I have heard yet. It is in keeping with other efforts which have been made.
As I said, we get down to one simple principle of whether this is an abdication of parliamentary powers, which I say it is. If so, should it be for an indefinite, uncertain period or should it be for a definite period? That is what we are asking, that that be done. It is all right to talk about the defence of Canada. We are all unanimous in that; we all subscribe to that; we are all ready to do everything possible for that. But what are we defending by doing these things? We are defending a way of life which we have known, which we have developed, which we have inherited. Part of that way of life, at least in so far as I see it, is this principle
Defence Production Act of parliamentary government, the supremacy of parliament, the absolute supremacy of parliament.
Personally I am not interested in the building of radar stations and thermonuclear weapons and all the other bits of pomp and circumstance we hear about if in bringing these things about we have to give up this important principle. I think we can do them both. I think we can maintain our way of life and at the same time be strong, as we all want to be. We know today that the best defence is to be able to strike back if necessary. I believe that we are in that position, and we want to remain so. I am sure that that is the feeling of the members of all parties in this house.
Surely we can reconcile that. Surely we are making a reasonable proposition. The proposition made this morning by the minister offered some concession, but as I heard it I do not think that it goes any further than to give us the right of debate, which we now have on moving a motion to go into supply, which would permit a debate. We can always have a debate on the motion to go into supply, or we can have a debate in supply itself.
We want a definite time limit placed on certain of these powers. We want the minister to have to come before parliament and justify their continuance. If he does not do that, if he fails to do that, or if he does not ask that it be done, then they will automatically expire. This principle has been established in other legislation of this type. I think the minister would enhance his own reputation and would at least show that he has learned something about the supremacy of parliament, which he modestly said he did not understand, if he would agree to such a proposal or to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), who spoke earlier this morning. The hon. member suggested three alternatives, any one of which would meet the purpose. They would detract nothing from the powers of the minister, but they would maintain a principle which means a great deal to many of us. Unless it is recognized, it will mean that this debate will have to be carried on much longer than otherwise would be the case.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not intend to delay the house very long as I expect to finish before one o'clock. I should like to review briefly the arguments which have been placed before the house in an attempt to bring this debate to a close. I do not know that that can be done, but I think it is only right that we

Defence Production Act have the privilege of reviewing some of the things which have been said and in the light of those statements try to come to a conclusion.
As reported on page 836 of Hansard of 1951, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated that these extraordinary powers should not be permanent. Then as reported on page 1961 of Hansard of this year the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) stated likewise. The minister also said in this debate that either we have a Defence Production Act with all of these powers or we have no act at all.
It has been said that one method of dealing with this matter would be to take it up when the reports are brought in or when the estimates are before us. Everyone knows the limitations of discussion at that time.
There is no argument as to whether the Department of Defence Production should have these powers; what is in question is whether they should have them as continuing powers. The red herrings which have been thrown across the path during the course of this debate seem to have been thrown there deliberately to confuse the issue. The issue is simply whether there should be a continuation of the extraordinary powers in the act.
I am sure that all hon. members of this house agree that the powers are needed. Those of us who are opposed to that portion of the bill which deals with section 41 of the act agree with the government that this department should be a permanent department. We agree that the salary of the minister of this department should conform with the salaries of other ministers. We agree that an emergency does exist and we agree also that extraordinary powers are needed. So we need not discuss those matters further.
I think we also agree that the presence of these extraordinary powers will bring results in almost every case without actually taking action. Therefore it is not a question of whether or not the powers are used; it is a question of whether the powers exist and are continuing. If you have a big enough club it is not always necessary to use that club.
I think that submission will take place without actually wielding the weapon. I do not believe that the statement made by the minister today changes our position to any great extent. All we say is that there should be an expiry date in respect to these extraordinary powers that are given in the bill, which would require that the minister come before parliament and place his case before parliament and that it be thoroughly reviewed in the light of existing circumstances.
[Mr. Leboe.l
Members on this side of the house have never said that the powers would not be granted to the minister when they were needed and as the emergency exists. It is only fair that the responsibility for the delay caused by this debate should rest squarely on the minister for insisting that there be a continuation of the powers, because I cannot conceive that this bill could not be brought down without having these powers continued. They could be limited, and the defence production department could still be on a permanent basis. Much has been said in the house about the opposition of many members to this bill, but we would be remiss in our duty if we did not take up the matter with vigilance and determination. The responsibility for the length of this debate rests fairly and squarely on the minister, who should bring down some amendment that will bring about an expiry date as far as the Defence Production Act is concerned relative to these extraordinary powers.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are being asked in the bill currently before us to continue in force indefinitely an act which, ruthlessly administered, could result in the completely dictatorial control of the entire Canadian economy. Apparently, judging from some of the arguments from the other side of the house, we are being asked to do this under the guise that an amiable, elderly gentleman is going to be the minister responsible for this act and that we can have complete confidence in him. Let me say at once that, while I think my first description was quite correct-"amiable and elderly"-he is also one of the great Canadians of all time.
When I was thinking of what I might say in connection with this bill, my mind went back to a time when I introduced him to a large gathering last autumn. In order to do justice to him, I read his obituary to that group of people. Famous Canadians have their obituaries written well in advance. I was quite happy to point out to them that the gentleman in question, while his obituary was read, was also present himself. That obituary pointed out one thing in connection with the Minister of Defence Production, Minister of Trade and Commerce and minister of almost everything. He had said to somebody at one point, following an unpleasant experience during wartime, that he felt he was living on borrowed time and that he wished to devote that time to the service of Canada. Those are thoughts that we cannot divorce from our minds when we consider this matter. We at times become a little confused because it is difficult to imagine this

particular minister using these powers to the detriment of our system of free government. But when we discuss the bill before us, we are not discussing it in the light of a particular person or of a particular time and place. We are discussing a measure which specifically will contain as far into the future as we can see a schedule of the most autocratic powers, a schedule of the most allembracing powers known in this country since this parliament came into existence.
I think the observations of the junior member for Halifax this morning became confused within this framework which I have just outlined, because he just could not see how it was possible for us on this side to admit on the one hand that the minister who would, for at least a few months, administer this act could be termed by us a great Canadian, a man who had made tremendous contributions in time of war and in time of peace to this country; and yet that we could also fear the autocratic aspects built into the act and the possibility that this minister or some other minister operating under this act might utilize those autocratic powers to the detriment of our country. The junior member for Halifax became confused in his own mind between opposition to unlimited powers indefinitely extended, which opposition certainly exists in this group, and opposition to arrangements for proper ordering of defence production in the light of circumstances presently existing, which opposition does not exist on this side of the house at this time.
I should like to give one further example of his confused thinking this morning before we break for lunch. I have searched the speech of the hon. member for Victoria-Carle-ton (Mr. Montgomery) back and forth with great care in an attempt to find some justification for the statement made by the hon. member for Halifax this morning, when he claimed that the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton said that we on this side of the house would give the minister anything he wants. From that he went ahead to the conclusion that the minister just wanted this act passed; therefore why did we not give it to him? Any hon. member who made a statement such as that made by the hon. member for Halifax this morning, completely without foundation in the printed record of this house, completely without substantiation, has very little cause to expect that we shall give much credence to his remarks.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the house took recess.
Defence Production Act The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before luncheon, when I was making my remarks, I made one small error in fact and I think perhaps I should correct it now. I have been informed that my reference to the hon. member for Halifax should have been to the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) and not to the junior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom). I am glad to make that correction. I may have been misled because of the calibre of his remarks rather than anything else but I realize that he has been here longer than has the other hon. gentleman.
I turn again to the argument which I was pursuing when the house rose for lunch. People might wonder why we object so strenuously to having these powers wrested from parliament itself and lodged in a particular minister. I think one of the reasons is contained in a comparatively brief quotation from one of the Speakers in the English house. It was Mr. Speaker Onslow who made this remark. While it was made many years before any of the gentlemen on the treasury benches came into this house, he might well have been thinking of certain of those gentlemen, perhaps even including the present Minister of Trade and Commerce and Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) when he said this:
Ministers seldom love parliament, never bring business there for counsel, but to carry points that must have the authority of the legislature; and in order to carry such points must previously strengthen themselves there by collecting all the force they can get for it.
There in one brief quotation is the substance of at least one argument for not wanting to see this power pass from parliament into the hands of any minister. Ministers do not love parliament. As to many ministers at least, if they can find a way of accomplishing something without coming here to parliament, they must be tempted-and very often yield to the temptation, as we have seen in the past-to follow other devious paths in accomplishing that which they wish to accomplish. Hence we find before us measures such as this Defence Production Act, which not only puts temptation in the way of the minister but practically begs him to by-pass parliament in order to accomplish certain things. I think we are quite right in looking askance at such measures.
Then again, Mr. Speaker, we must wonder about the field which the Defence Production Act covers. To many people in this country defence and defence production will be thought of in terms of guns, aeroplanes, ships and the factories in which to build them.

Defence Production Act That is perhaps the meaning of defence production on the face of it. But in a time when total war has come to mean something which affects every aspect of the community, we must realize that defence production affects every fibre of our community and every fibre of our nation, and that an act dealing with defence production must ultimately simmer down to and work into every aspect of our national life.
Let us think for a moment of some of the things which have come out in connection with defence purchases over a period of the last few years. We have seen the government buying for purposes of the defence operations of Canada such unlikely things as boudoir lamps, silk stockings, cameras, tooth brushes, soap and all these things in addition to those which, when we think about it for a moment, are obvious but which might not occur to us at first glance, such as food, in tremendous quantities and of all kinds. We know that in the United States, for example, one of the accoutrements of any well-equipped battleship is a soda fountain. I would presume that the Canadian soldier, wanting to be as well looked after as is his United States counterpart, would expect to be served ice cream cones. I would therefore imagine that it would be part of the responsibility of the defence production department, in their work-and quite properly so-to see that he receives his ice cream cone. But perhaps we do not realize that under the terms of this act which it is proposed to extend indefinitely the Minister of Defence Production could ultimately end up quite properly in the business of producing ice cream cones for the armed forces, or in the business of producing boudoir lamps, or in the business of producing silk stockings or anything else which it is conceivable that this nation could produce.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Don't forget underwear.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Thank you. As my friend to my immediate right among the government supporters points out, the government might even end up in the business of producing underwear. I do not quite know why he is so deeply interested in that matter, but I can tell him this. If he were in the underwear producing business, especially in the silk underwear business- because, after all, we have the WAC's-and if the government decided that they just did not like the colour of his output, or that they did not like the fit of it or, in fact, if they did not like my hon. friend himself, under the terms of this act they could move in overnight, appoint a controller, throw him out of his business and run the business to suit the government. Mr. Speaker, if there 

is anyone else who has any other field of endeavour that he would like to introduce into the argument at this stage, I should be glad to tell him what might happen to him under the terms of this act.
Again, Mr. Speaker, there has been so much detailed examination of some of the clauses of this bill that we may have lost sight, in plain, simple English, of some of the principal things which it will empower the Minister of Defence Production to do at any time in the future as long as we can foresee. For example, the Minister of Defence Production is in a position to override completely the civil service. For purposes of this department of his he can hire whom he wishes, how he wishes and at the salary he wishes. We might remind ourselves again that he can appoint anyone in this great country of ours to exercise any one of these powers. As I said a few minutes ago, he can buy, acquire and control anything in the country. He can enter into any business operation. He can stockpile any commodity. So far as defence procurement is concerned, I think the simplest thing is to say that his powers are unlimited. He has $100 million made available immediately to do these things.
The Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), when he thinks that something is necessary and vital, and according to his judgment alone, can enter into any contract without any responsibility save the responsibility of reporting the contract to the governor in council after it has been entered into. He can abrogate any responsibility for royalties. Long after an agreement is entered into in perfect good faith by a person who believes that the government should keep its word, he can even renegotiate the contract and remove any of its provisions or protections, most specifically the protection regarding price written into the contract.
In order to do all these things he of course must be in a position to force compliance with his desires, and he is in a position so to do. He can appoint a controller to operate any business, even, as my friend said a few minutes ago, a silk underwear business. He can invest public money in any business in the form of loans, but above all-and this is the point I should like to examine for a few minutes-by this measure the governor in council can disregard any statute passed by this house, any statute passed by a provincial legislature anywhere in Canada, and any agreement entered into by anybody. It seems to me that is the most complete negation that we have known in peacetime of everything for which a free democracy stands.

Here is a situation in which parliament, the representatives of the people, a group who speak for the people and have been called to this house by all the citizens of this nation over the age of 21, having made their desires known, having done what they as a group felt and believed was right, can have their decisions completely negatived and disregarded by one man and one man alone. What about the governor in council? Well, what responsibility has the governor in council to this house save to report actions once they have taken place? This house has no knowledge beforehand of what the governor in council proposes. There is no way by which the house can control these actions. The most we can expect as to the governor in council is the right of review, so to speak, and even that is a difficult process.
As I have said, I should like somebody on the government side of the house to stand up and give instances if they can, of other free democratic countries-they can of course find many cases under dictatorships-where the governor in council in peacetime has been given the right indefinitely to overrule, override and disregard the wishes of parliament and the statutes passed by that body. I can understand that a measure such as this would have an appeal to certain people and to a certain type of thinking. It has an appeal of ruthless efficiency to ruthless officials to whom it matters not how they accomplish what they want to accomplish as long as they can accomplish it, who do not care who is trampled under in the process or what we lose. We might well consider that in the battle for freedom being waged by all our free democracies at the present time one of the dangers facing us is that we may lose our freedom in the very process of defending it.
As I understand the situation, that is the basis of the minister's presentation of the bill. He says to us that in order to preserve our freedom in the event of war, in order that we may be able to wage war as efficiently as possible, it is necessary for us to sacrifice rights for which we and those who have gone before us have fought and died for hundreds of years. I do not think there is any great advantage to be gained by sacrificing freedom now in order to defend freedom later. I think there is perhaps a reasonable possibility that there is one case where we can have our cake and eat it too, certainly a case where we can have our freedom now and still be in a position to defend it should the need arise.
When I was thinking about the bill one thing about which I wondered was why the
Defence Production Act masses of the people of Canada had not been more perturbed over the issue, why it was that in the months elapsing between the presentation of the resolution and the presentation of the bill there had not been more public controversy over the issue, and why it was left particularly to this group in the house to fight hard in defence of the freedoms of our country. My mind went back to a book I read not too long ago entitled "1984", which is a rather terrifying picture of the sort of society to which a bill such as the one now before us will lead. In two sentences in that book is found an explanation of why we as a group feel so keenly about this matter and why there is not yet the public protest about it that there should be. I read:
In a way, the world view of the Party-
With a capital "p".
-imposed itself most successfully on people incapable of understanding it. They could be made to accept the most flagrant violations of reality, because they never fully grasped the enormity of what was demanded of them, and were not sufficiently interested in public events to notice what was happening.
I think we have a roughly similar situation here. The amending bill currently before the house is short. The act amended is long. It is a complicated subject, one which the average person, not called here to study and be aware of these things, might quite reasonably not know very much about. But I do feel that as the words of this debate, and they have been many, seep through, as the press, radio and magazines of this country do their job in bringing to the people of Canada the story of what is happening in this House of Commons at this time, the people will come to the almost unanimous conclusion that if this bill passes in its present form their basic liberties to conduct themselves as free men and to carry on their affairs as free men will have been seriously hampered and greatly reduced. They will have been reduced, Mr. Speaker, not for the reasons which are genuinely justifiable but reduced because of some undefinable emergency which the minister has held out as one of the main reasons for the necessity for this measure at this time.
I would not think there is anyone in this house who feels secure and completely happy about international affairs today. But 1 would not think there is anyone in this house either who feels we are in the same perilous position we were in in 1951 when this measure first came into being. Perhaps more than any time, except during an actual war, 1951 did mark a genuine state of emergency, and imminent emergency. I think

Defence Production Act perhaps there is a great difference between an emergency and an imminent emergency, and 1951 marked a time of imminent emergency. It marked a time when, almost from day to day, we did not know what might happen. In 1955, with the measure still having a year to run, we have reached a stage of uneasy peace. I believe that term has been used many times by both the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and other people in other countries who occupy a position similar to his. We have reached a stage where men of good will feel there is a reasonable possibility of securing peace if we continue to travel the paths which we are now following. Where then is the claim of emergency which would cause us to introduce powers such as those contained in this bill?
In our thinking, in our planning and in our attitudes in this house, Mr. Speaker, we have to stick to the basic principles of democracy. Today, all too often I am afraid, the government which is in power and the ministers who occupy the treasury benches come before us feeling that their long tenure of office and their success at the polls qualifies them and makes them right in throwing aside the basic ideas, basic concepts and departing on new, untried and different paths. In many cases they get away with it. However, these measures, these attitudes and actions are written into the history of this nation. We cannot see their effect immediately. None of us can look too far into the future. But when we depart from things which men have held right, proper and good for century after century, we embark upon a course which has tremendous dangers in it.
Now, if there is a necessity for taking these powers, if there is a necessity for taking a chance, let us chance it. But unless that necessity is clear and evident, let us not sacrifice that which we know to be right, that which we know to be proper. As Lord Acton once said in the house in England:
The one thing that saved England from the fate of other countries was not her insular position, nor the independent spirit nor the magnanimity of her people-for we have been proud of the despotism we obeyed under the Tudors, and not ashamed of the tyranny we exercised in our dependencies-but only the consistent, uninventive, stupid fidelity to that political system which originally belonged to all the nations that traversed the ordeal of feudalism.
Perhaps we on this side of the house may be charged with all those unfair adjectives, but we are consistently true to a political system in which we believe. We are not supporters of the throwing aside of the system nor the pandering to the desires of one man, no matter how amiable he may be and no matter what his past record may be.
[Mr. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace) .1
Then again, Mr. Speaker, as we go back along the highway of history to the time of the early Romans we can see that this danger has been evident almost from time immemorial. In the letters of Junius, we find this:
We can never be really in danger till the forms of parliament are made use of to destroy the substance of our civil and political liberties: till parliament itself betrays its trust by contributing to establish new principles of government, and employing the very weapons committed to it by the collective body to stab the constitution.
We stand here, almost at the crossroads of our democratic system of government. In my estimation this parliament is being asked to pass a bill which betrays the trust the people of Canada have reposed in it, to betray this trust by establishing a new principle of government. If this act is continued indefinitely and written into the law of this land without some reservation therein, that will be a new principle of government. This fact was clearly indicated earlier today when the minister himself came into the house and proposed a tawdry, paltry, tiny concession, but at least again it was a new method of dealing with the public business of this country, made necessary by a new concept in government, by a new approach and by the very bill which so many people on the government side have tried to present to us as nothing more or less than the logical outgrowth of an emergency which does not exist.
I, for one, do not want to have any part in stabbing this house in the back, or in stabbing in the back the democratic institutions of this country which have brought us freedom, self-respect and the life we know today. Because I would not have any part in such a stabbing in the back, Mr. Speaker, I shall vote against this bill.
