speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak against Bill No. 256 because I believe it is dynamite. The minister has said that it is a simple bill. Certainly it is a very brief one.
The second part to which we object has only eight little words, and it is in those eight little words that we find the dynamite that could be used against democracy by any man or any government that is given such power. No other democratic country in the world has such an act permanently on its statute books.
In his book "Government and Parliament", Right Hon. Herbert Morrison tells of a similar bill which he was authorized to prepare when the socialists were in power in Britain. Britain's emergency powers defence acts of 1945 were limited to five years, just as our Defence Production Act was. After those five years Great Britain's emergency act could be renewed year by year. Naturally the socialists would prefer such powers to be permanent because that is the first step in state domination. Naturally the socialists want to give such powers to the government because if they ever got into power themselves

Defence Production Act it would then be very easy to nationalize industry. But it is hard to understand why a so-called tree enterprise government would want to show such contempt for .parliament.
We are being asked to grant these extensive powers and in so doing we must rely on the whim of one man, the right hon. minister. He has told us that he does not propose to be told now by any hon. member just when he will or should liquidate the act. He has told us, "Either we have a Defence Production Act with all these powers or we have no act at all." In all these things that the minister keeps telling us, the rights of parliament seem to have been completely bypassed.
We have been told that there is not the slightest suggestion that personal liberties or freedoms will be menaced, but I think that would depend upon what you call personal liberties or freedoms. Through Bill No. 256 a government could achieve a socialist revolution without any consultation or by-your-leave of parliament. That is why this group to my left is so happy with the minister's bill.
That is why the socialist government in Britain back in 1949 authorized Mr. Herbert Morrison to prepare a bill like this, a bill which would empower the government to govern by regulation in peacetime rather than through the orthodox if sometimes cumbersome machinery of parliament. However, before Mr. Morrison had finished drafting his bill another election took place in Great Britain and the socialist majority was reduced to six. In his book "Government and Parliament" Mr. Morrison told what happened to his bill. Referring to the parliament of 1950-51 he said:
We could not proceed with what would probably have been a controversial measure because our majority had been reduced to six. However, the draft bill is in the archives as a basis of consideration by ministers at any time.
As long as there is a free enterprise Conservative government in Great Britain I am sure that that bill will remain in the archives. But not so in Canada. A so-called free enterprise government is asking, or perhaps I should say demanding, that parliament give these sweeping powers to the government. These powers are to be permanent. It seems to me that they eat away at the very foundation of our constitution.
Why is this government asking for such powers at this time? We have not had much explanation. Back in 1951 when the Defence Production Act, with its five-year time limit, was introduced and passed we were at war in Korea. Today we are not at war anywhere. The minister has been suggesting that there is an emergency which necessitates that

these powers be given the government at this time, and for all time to come.
The minister has been scornfully hinting that the opposition does not know what is going on in the world, but what the minister seems to forget is that this all-wise government is not parliament. We in the opposition are also part of our democratic system. If there are things going on in the world that demand such revolutionary powers being placed in the hands of one man the opposition should be told about those things rather than just having them called an emergency.
Strangely enough, while the Minister of Defence Production is hinting at a dire emergency which necessitates that these sweeping powers be given him, his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), is suggesting that there is some improvement in world conditions. In Paris on May 9 he said that the international situation, at least in Europe, was improved, and he has been saying that many times here in Canada. While the Minister of Defence Production is riding roughshod over parliament the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) is saying, and I quote from the foreword of Current Affairs for June 1955 as follows:
We in Canada value the essential freedoms which make up our way of life even more than we value life itself. We are joined with those who think as we do in a colossal effort, through the medium of the United Nations and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, to preserve those freedoms, peacefully if we may-by force of arms if we must.
We on this side of the house have a feeling that the minister is not having too tranquil a time in his own backyard over this sweeping bill. There must be quite a few freedom-loving government members who view this bill with alarm. But the right hon. minister will get his bill through. When the Defence Production Act first came before this house in 1951 the leader of the Conservative party had this to say, as reported on page 849 of Hansard of March 2, 1951:
In describing the bill, the minister frankly stated that it contained powers of an extraordinary nature; but, as has been pointed out, there was no explanation as to why those extraordinary powers are required at this time to do the things we all agree should be done, and very quickly. The obvious fact is that the minister sees no reason to explain. The government has a huge majority. The minister decided that this should be done, he obtains the consent of the government, and he knows that the vote will support what is before this house. Consequently the rest of us, and I suppose the members of his party as well, have no need to be told why action of this kind should be taken at this time. Surely in the light of what is before us there can be no other explanation of the fact that powers so wide as these should be required.
The right hon. minister will get his bill through. He will override Her Majesty's

loyal opposition just as he has probably overridden his own colleagues, but not before we in the opposition have voiced our united disapproval. The odds are certainly against us. The government majority is too strong; but
. . . how can man die better Than facing fearful odds
For the ashes of his fathers,
And the temples of his gods?
What does this bill mean to Canadians? It means that the entire economy and manpower of Canada are being placed in the hands of one man, the Minister of Defence Production. The minister has modestly pointed out that he knows more than any other man in the world about defence purchasing, and that I am sure is true. On this side of the house many hon. members have paid tribute to the minister because we also have a high opinion of his experience and ability. But life is not stationary; ministers come and go, and so do governments. I ask the minister, and perhaps I am asking too much of his imagination: what if a socialist government should come into power in this country, which is a pretty wild flight of fantasy, I know. But one has only to witness the approval of the group to my left to realize how the minister is playing into the hands of socialism.
I should like to take a look at section 30, in which the governor in council may designate as an essential material any material or substance, the control, supply and use of which is in his opinion essential to ensure the availability of adequate defence supplies, etc. What does that mean? As a journalist, I looked to see what section 30 could do to our cherished freedom of the press. I think this is a familiar phrase to the minister. What is to stop the minister from tampering with the freedom of the press? It is true that he could not censor the actual copy that goes into a newspaper. He would not wield an editor's blue pencil. But through section 30 he certainly could censor the press very forcibly. If the governor in council wanted to designate newsprint as an essential material, what is to stop him? That could be a potent weapon in censorship of our press.
What is to stop the Minister of Defence Production from interfering with labour contracts? What is to stop him from moving in on any plant, any industry, any property -real or personal-under the guise of a defence project?
As I said at the outset, no other democratic country in the world has given such dictatorial powers to one man or government. I do not see how any hon. member who cherishes freedom can vote for this bill, with its sweeping and permanent powers.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs is spending laborious days trying with all his might to extend the rule of law throughout the world; yet he is going to be asked to vote for a measure which threatens the rule of law here among us. We have the Prime Minister, whom I am going to quote in a moment in addresses to the bar association. I hope that is all right, Mr. Speaker. I want to show what a great defender of the rule of law the Prime Minister has been in years past, and what an eloquent one. Then I am going to ask why he is not here to speak. I am going to challenge him to speak. If it is not disrespectful, I am going to demand that he speak.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Good; that is better.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I think we are entitled to hear from him in this matter. I would not regard the Minister of Defence Production as a great expert on the rule of law because I doubt whether he is interested in it. The Prime Minister is a different cup of tea. The Prime Minister ought to be the keeper of the conscience, so to speak, of this house. If we
4710	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act are wrong in what we are saying, he ought to come and tell us why we are wrong. Meanwhile I should like to quote from the Prime Minister. This goes back quite a while. He was addressing the bar association in 1931. He was then a leading lawyer and a distinguished authority on matters of law. He said this:
To none as thoroughly as to the men of our profession has history taught the lesson that constant vigilance is the price of liberty.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister to read that sentence and then to read to himself section 27 of the act, which states:
(1) Where the minister is satisfied that (a) a person who has entered into a defence contract has failed or is likely to fail to perform the contract in a businesslike and efficient manner . . .
I like that language, "has failed or is likely to fail". The minister can take action not merely on what has happened but on what he thinks is likely to happen. Then it is interesting to observe that if he is not satisfied-
. . . the minister may authorize another person [DOT] . . to carry on, until the minister otherwise directs, the whole or any part of the business of that person.
That is an interesting power. I heard an interesting illustration of that power given one day. I have not the details, but the gist of the story was this; it was illustrating the powers in that section. It had to do with a case where some producer was called upon to undertake a certain contract. As the story came to me, this was in the morning about nine o'clock. Apparently he showed some hesitation. I did not gather that it was more than that. But according to the way the story went, he was then reminded that there was a train leaving for his city at twelve o clock and that if he did not make up his mind to do what was wanted, on that twelve o clock train there would be a man with power to take over his plant.
I would imagine that sort of thing has seldom happened. The minister has told us that he uses these powers very little and that he wants them as a stand-by. But that story is interesting. It is an interesting comment on the way in which we live. I never would have believed it was necessary in peacetime or in anything short of a violent emergency to have action of that kind taken. But there it is.
I come to another quotation from the Prime Minister. I only wish he were here to listen to these fine statements which he made in the days of his legal distinction. He was speaking to the bar association, and he had this to say about lawyers in the province of Quebec:
Of course he recognizes that certain conceptions are inexorably established . . . The untrammelled 

freedom of creating contractual relations and so making laws binding on oneself and on all others who have consented thereto . . . The complete liability to repair all injuries wrongfully caused to another .	. Such are some of the cardinal
principles which he and his code have regarded as necessary postulates.
Following that I should like to ask the Prime Minister to look at section 32, which
says:
Every person who . . .
(c) wilfully obstructs a controller in the exercise of any of his functions ... is guilty of an offence.
The Minister of Defence Production referred to that in his speech and pointed out that there is a certain softening, shall I say, of the provision; with respect to a person who has been charged with an offence because he has not exercised due diligence I would refer to subsection 5 of section 32, which reads in part:
. . . in any proceeding against a person who was a director or officer of a corporation when the corporation committed an offence under this act for being a party to and guilty of such offence, the burden of proving his absence of such knowledge or the exercise of such due diligence by him is upon the accused.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the draftsman remembered that the thing had to be weighted against the citizen and in favour of the arbitrary power. I said a moment ago that this was the first time that arbitrary power had been made permanent. I want to refer for a moment to the time the act was passed. I am reading now from the minister's speech of June 7, at page 4510 of Hansard. He said then:
The statement I made in 1951-
That was his statement indicating that it was hoped this would be temporary, which induced us not to oppose it.
-was made in good faith, in the earnest hope that we would now be living in a world in which normal peacetime conditions would prevail. Such is not the case, and it is in the light of present day circumstances that 1 am compelled to recommend the continuation of the Defence Production Act in its present form.
The minister is not going to ask us to believe that in 1951 he had any expectation that we would have emerged into a nice, cosy, peaceful, snug, quiet world in five years. Everyone who knew his onions in 1951 knew there was no hope that we would get away from a tense situation. I am not going to take time to argue how much more or less tense it is now than in 1951. What I am arguing is that an emergency cannot go on forever. Can an emergency go on for 10, 20 or 30 years? When does the abnormal become normal? Are we going to upset our whole way of life and resort to arbitrary

power for a 30 or 40 year emergency? As I say, I think the minister did himself an injustice. He does not usually live in the clouds.
I want to say a word about the rule of law.
It is not just a lot of picayune little rules for this or that. It is really the embodiment of the Christian ethic in practical form. It is the thing we live by, the thing by which our relations with each other are governed, At page 193 of "Law of the Constitution" Dicey says:
We mean when we speak of the rule of law not only that with us no man is above the law but what is a different thing, that here every man ... is subject to the ordinary law of the realm and amenable to the jurisdiction of the ordinary tribunals.
As against that consider the unlimited powers given by the act. The rule of law is the greatest practical exposition and achievement of Christianity. It is the real cornerstone of our civilization. We have inherited it and we should cling to it. It is the binder and cement of our civilization.
May I now say a word about the powers, and I shall be very brief. The minister indicated the way the act was brought about. He said it was based on the final edition of the munitions and supply act passed in 1939. Then he said, "We believe it is a model act". As I have already said, it certainly is a model act from the point of view of the aims of those who drew it. There is virtually unlimited power over the economic life of Canada. If the scope of the bill covered just a minor area of our economic life, let us say the building of elevators, we might swallow it; but read the definitions of defence projects, defence supplies, essential materials and all the long list. Read section 11, under which the minister may organize the whole economic life of Canada in so far as it is concerned with defence, and ask yourselves what there is in a modern state preparing for war that is not concerned with defence or cannot be made to look like it. The section gives virtual control over the Canadian economy.
I have referred to section 27 and the threat to take over a plant. I now refer to section 32 where it is an offence even to have a mind of your own or even to suggest you want to have a mind of your own. What the section says is that every person who wilfully obstructs a controller in the exercise of any of his functions under section 27 is guilty of an offence. I suppose a controller is one of those people appointed by the minister, who has the right to appoint anyone with all
Defence Production Act the powers to do things that he himself has. That is in section 5, which reads:
The minister may authorize any person, on his behali and under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
That is only where the
person who has entered into the defence contract has failed or is likely to fail to perform the contract.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I have covered that. I referred to that before. Make your own speech.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You left out part of the quotation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Note the minister's delightful power of being able to anticipate the future. The minister points out that a man can have an appeal to the courts. That is true. After he has suffered injury and been treated in this arbitrary manner he may_ go to the courts. It will take him some time and some money, and he will have high priced counsel fighting against him, part of whose fees, incidentally, he will pay as a taxpayer.
One more excuse the minister gives is that the powers have not been used. I fully accept this explanation of that, of course, and in answer I only wish to quote the remarks of a very great man who had a great deal to do with setting up the rule of law by which we are governed. He said this:
Necessity is the plea lor every infringement of human freedom; it is the argument of tyrants; it is the creed of slaves.
The minister says he could not carry on without these powers. He has had 40 years of experience and he knows the story. I think too well of the minister to believe that he could not carry on without them. He has not asked us to believe that it is hard to place contracts. Why would it be hard? Is his money not good? Is the government money not good? Are order books so bursting with orders now? Are commodities so scarce now that he is going to have any difficulty? Is there no unemployment? Still he asks us to believe that he could not carry on efficiently without the act.
My belief is that the minister wants these powers in the act just because he wants them. He likes them. He felt lonely when he did not have them for a short time. The powers must be there in his hands. But they can have evil results. When they get on the statute books they have a way of staying there. They may be left there until people we did not anticipate come along and use them for purposes which we would not like.

Defence Production Act
Our socialist friends would be entirely pleased with them if they ever came into power. I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will not disagree with me. I am sure he loves these powers. Under them you can punish people; you can get after the wicked people the socialists see behind every bush.
My time is running out, and I am sure the minister wants to hear the rest of what I have to say. If I thought that giving the minister what he wants would not do any harm I would be inclined to go a long way with him, but what is going to happen is that very soon we will have a generation who will not know anything different, to whom this will be the normal way of life. They will read the bill with all these powers, but they will not go back to the debate of 1951 and find out that they were, so to speak, extorted from us by assurances that the world was coming to an end, that the government could not possibly get on without them, that there were material shortages, and so on and so on.
The minister has been working under this act for four years now. He has been very frank in telling us he has had little or no trouble. He has told us how little the powers were used. I was not in the house the other day when the hon. member for Eglinton questioned him, but my understanding is that he said some of these powers had not been needed. I believe there was some question as between the word "needed" and "used". I will use the word "needed".
There is one thing that must have been interesting and perhaps satisfying to the minister, and that is the allies he has on this measure. As I said a moment ago, the socialists love this; it is right down their alley. It is a curious bit of irony that a so-called Liberal government should be producing this reactionary measure.

speechtext: That is a secret of course, which we are not allowed to know. Perhaps there are Tories who believe in these principles, but happily they are not on this side now. I will answer that another day. At page 405 of "The Conservative Mind" he is quoted as saying:
The new state-
That would be the socialist state.
-will also directly augment authority and social pressure by new powers of punishment and compulsion. So far from withering away, as in theory both the individualist and the total state should, the new state, if it is to bring into being and serve the better society, must create new offences and punish them.
The word "offences" interested me because we have it here in this act. While I do not suppose many people have been prosecuted, the power is always there.
I said when I began that I hoped we would carry on this debate to the very last moment we could, in the hope that we may arouse interest outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Don't get discouraged; the bell will not save you for a few minutes.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I think I am doing all right. I just want to be sure that I am not leaving out any of my best points that the minister may want to hear.
Once since I have been here it has happened that the press has interested the people of Canada in a measure, to such an extent that within two weeks the government had to bend the knee. It was a little thing. I believe it had to do with tenders in the Department of Public Works. It was very interesting to see what public opinion could do. That was one time when I felt the opposition had done something that almost entitled it to get into a textbook. When the matter came before the house the opposition complained. The press and the public became interested and within two weeks the government had to go into reverse. I therefore do not abandon hope.
I believe this bill-I do not wish to sound extravagant or exaggerated-may be the parting of the ways as between the permanence of arbitrary powers and the kind of society in which we have lived and which we describe as living under the rule of law. This means that men have their rights which cannot be overridden by the arbitrary powers of others; they are sacred, protected properly by law.
No one can deny that this act bristles with arbitrary powers. They stick out all over.
I am not saying there might not be an argument which would make us say, "Yes, we hate these powers, but nevertheless we must concede them". No such argument has been

made. It seems to me that no argument even approaching it has been made, except that the minister has cited his 40 years of experience as authority for the proposition. At page 4512 of Hansard for June 7 the minister said:
I have had a great deal of experience in buying for governments.
I agree.
I started some 40 years ago as a consulting engineer, and I have been doing some buying for governments ever since. I can tell this house that generally speaking a government order does not receive the same attention as a privately placed order. The reason is that generally speaking the government cannot put on as much pressure as does the private buyer.
I would bet a small sum, Mr. Speaker

I am a cautious man-that the minister can get his orders executed. In my opinion that statement comes perilously close to nonsense. It comes close to nonsense for the minister to ask us to pass a measure which is the embodiment of arbitrary powers, and to have no better special reason to give us than that. We are to take his word because he says the powers are needed. If the minister gave me his word about the construction of an elevator or a tank, that would be all right. However, when it comes to the rule of law we know the minister is not interested. We know the things the minister has said and believes: "If we wanted to get away with it, who would stop us?", and on another occasion, "If we have overstepped our powers, I make no apology for having done so." It is tiresome, to bring up these quotations again but they should be brought out because they are relevant. It is to this man we are asked to give these arbitrary powers. It does not make sense to me.
It is hard to carry on this struggle.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext: It is hard to carry on an argument when there is no argument-

speechtext: It is hard to carry on this struggle because we know there are a lot of people in this house whose minds are closed.

speechtext:
I am doing pretty well so far. We always hope there may be people on the outside whose minds are not closed. There is the press. We can hope that the press, as on a previous occasion, may catch the public interest. The pulpit should be interested in this. Everyone should be interested in the fight for freedom and the battle against arbitrary powers. What about the universities? What about the professors everywhere? There are one or two of them
Defence Production Act in this house, and I hope to hear from them soon. Why should they not take part in this debate?
Happily there is some sign of a little cracking. We were not extended that phony olive branch that we got this morning because the government were entirely satisfied with the situation. The only reason they did that was because they hoped we might be suckers and take it, thus ending this debate. We have that small satisfaction. If we go on, who knows; perhaps we might get a real concession. Perhaps the people on the other side who agree with me-and I know there are some-will become vocal, not necessarily in the house but perhaps in caucus or in council. I firmly believe that we are right. I do not usually like to be with the minority opinion, but in this case I am content.
Not only do I believe we are right, but I believe there has not been a real exercise of judgment on the part of the public in connection with this matter. I still hope there may be. The press could do it in a week, or they could do it in less than a week as they did before, if we are able to make them believe-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: That is the thing.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I would not expect the good doctor to be very much interested.
^ Mr. McCann: I would be very interested if you could make them believe.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
We hope to make them believe. We are not doing this for fun. It is hot weather, and not all of us enjoy the favourable circumstance of living in Ottawa. There are signs that the press are beginning to be interested, and we can only hope that will continue. For that reason, so far as I am concerned, I am ready to continue. We hope we still may convince the people of Canada that this is a serious matter. We hope we may convince them so that if they do not take action now they may take it later; and one day they may come to our assistance and force this government, which has misappropriated the word "Liberal", to live up to the implications of the name they so unworthily bear.
I said it could be done, and so it could, if only we can convince the press that there is no question here of defence. We are all one about that. There is no question here about the minister not being able to get permanent tenure for his civil servants. We are all agreed about that. Do not let us cloud the issue with nonsense of that kind.
We have shown in the past that we are very ready to give substantial powers when they are needed. There is no dispute about

Defence Production Act that. But now we are asked to instal permanently in the legislation of this house a measure which four years ago we refrained from voting against because there was a great emergency, and on the ground that it was to be temporary now to have the government come along with what I call effrontery and ask us, four years later, when the work of the department is settling down and it is pursuing its normal course, to adopt this measure which four years ago was commended to us as temporary and to take off the time limit and to ask that it be made permanent, is just too much. As I say, I hope we shall carry this on to the bitter end.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the opposition to my right have been more or less beating a dead horse in the hope that some of their press barons will take it up and try to stir up support for this issue. I do not intend to support the Liberal government in any way because I think it is equally guilty in this respect.
I could not help but notice the number of times the hon. member for Greenwood spoke of the rule of law in the course of his remarks. He more or less emphasized that as our way of life and the whole basis of this discussion. It is rather incongruous to find hon. members to my right rising in their places time and time again, trying to indicate their interest in protecting the people of this nation. For my part I think they are part and parcel of the kind of program which eventually will not only lead this country into trouble in the struggle for a free world, by taking our resources and using them purely for profit. It seems to me that the hon. member for Greenwood spoke not only for St. James street and Bay street but for Wall street as well.
It is well known that at the beginning of the war, in 1939, the friends of the Conservative party, and indeed the people who were ready to profiteer, showed no readiness to assist in the defence of this country by producing the goods that were needed for that purpose at that time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: What is the evidence of that?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I can
prove it, Mr. Speaker. I am making my speech. In 1939 the Canadian parliament passed an act having to do with the production of war materials, guaranteeing a 5 per cent profit to the companies that would produce the necessities of war.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: That was when the C.C.F. did not want one man to go.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Your party said they did not want to have anything to do with it at all.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
We are
very proud of what this party did. We are proud not only of our party's attitude but of the participation of the members of the C.C.F. party in the defence of the country both here and abroad. In 1939 the companies of this country were not prepared to produce for its protection. A few months later, namely on August 26, this parliament was informed that the companies were not doing their share in the production of defence materials.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Name the companies. What companies were these?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Apparently they were many of the friends of the opposition to my right, because parliament was concerned and moved to take the 5 per cent ceiling off the profits of these companies. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in answer to a question by Mr. T. C. Douglas, the then member for Weyburn, said this, and I quote from Hansard:
I can say to my hon. friend that from that day to this the defence purchasing board has done its very best to place contracts on that basis and has used every pressure that could be brought to bear in the form of patriotism and so on, but to date it has not succeeded in placing a single contract on that basis.
We find our hon. friends to the right rising in their places day after day and belabouring the government because it wishes to give the minister power to get the necessary defence materials in the event of an emergency. Unless the hon. member for Greenwood is trying to straddle the fence, he has indicated that we are not in an emergency period. Just a few weeks ago some members of parliament were taken on a flight to Churchill. There we were shown the situation which exists in the northern part of our country. Just a few short months ago the government had to take the responsibility of building an early warning line against invading aircraft. In spite of the fact that they had to go there in the winter and travel over the tundra in snowmobiles and set up their radar stations, before we got back to Ottawa we were informed, whether or not it is true, that this country could be invaded by a new type of guided missile against which we would not be protected by the radar screen in the northern part of our country.
The issue is not whether the Minister of Defence Production should or should not have the right to procure the necessities for defence, but rather one which is more crucial. Before expressing my own point of view, may I say I believe the announcement the minister

made this morning will amply cover the situation. He will place before the house the various contracts which are let, and ten members will be able to rise in their places and demand that the contracts be reviewed by the house within a matter of six months. I think that will give parliament the right to screen and investigate the procurement contracts which come from the minister's department.
This whole problem goes much deeper than that; it is much more basic. I am thinking of the causes of war and the necessity of this parliament giving the minister the powers for which he asks. It is quite true that we all hope for universal and lasting peace. At the same time we realize that we are in for a long period of unsettled times that may project itself far into the distant future.
If I tried to be elected for any one particular reason more than another it was to do what I could to try to erase the causes of modern warfare. Along with the rest of the C.C.F. group I think the only basis on which the democratic nations of the western hemisphere can initiate a program to gradually move toward universal peace is to eliminate the profit motive. I am saying that as long as we have the profit motive, which is supported by hon. members to my right and by the Social Credit group to my left, and indeed by the government itself, we are never going to remove the base cause of war. Today the base cause of war is profit; it was profit in 1914-18, it was profit in 1939 and it is profit today.
Hon. members to my right talk about fear psychology and war psychology, but there are none worse than themselves and the people who support them in causing the fear psychology which grips people throughout the world. Until we can eliminate the possibility of making a profit out of this sort of thing, then I am saying we are not going to find a basis for peace. The negotiators across the conference table at the league of nations were bedevilled by the fact that the press of the world and the warmongers of the world were creating this fear psychology.
May I say to the hon. member who seems to want to interrupt that of course Russia is dangerous to the peace of the world, and will be for a long time. But I say to him that until we hit at the root cause of war in our own country and set up our economy on a peacetime basis we will not be able to defend ourselves against the growing menace of communism. We have not been able to do it in the past five years.
Consider the situation today in Europe and Asia. Even with all our diplomatic measures we have not succeeded. Until we get down
Defence Production Act to the basis of organizing our economy for peacetime, when the production of the workers and the farmers can go into an increased living standard, when we can use our production in order to help less fortunate people in the world and do away with the fundamental basic cause of war, which is the profit motive, we will never have peace.
As I said at the beginning, this is more than a matter of parliamentary procedure. We have the power to investigate any expenditure made by the Minister of Defence Production. We have the right in parliament to look at every expenditure made by the government. We have the right to ask the minister to bring his expenditures before us and his methods of procurement. In the interests of democracy I think it is much better that we have that right and that the minister have the power in these emergent times to say to private enterprise, "We need these items of procurement, we are going to have them at a certain price, and if necessary we will ask you to start producing them."
I know full well that many examples could be cited since 1945 where this government has used patronage or perhaps bad judgment, but in any case we know that under the profit motive considerable extra cost enters into our defence requirements. More and more this government should try to have crown corporations for the production of our defence needs, so we could eliminate the abuses that have occurred in the past.
I could quote excerpts from Hansard of May 6, 1953, page 4878, to show that contracts have been given which seemed rather stupid, rather exorbitant and without any foundation of necessity. From April 1, 1951, to December 31, 1952, the government purchased certain items for the women in the armed services, who at that time numbered 3,447. During that time they purchased 44,440 raincoats at a cost of $924,527, or 12 for each woman in the services. They purchased 96,663 hats at a cost of $186,485 or 27 hats for each woman in the armed services. During the same period for the 100,026 men in the services they purchased 1,340,873 pairs of leather footwear, or 13 pairs for each person. That shows the ridiculousness of it all. There were purchased 1,360,592 summer trousers, or 13 for each man in the services. There were purchased 2,817,633 suits of summer underwear, or 28 for each man in the services.
This simply indicates that if we had the purchasing of our defence requirements under public ownership I feel sure there would be no good reason for these ridiculous contracts being given to private enterprise.

Defence Production Act
Following the line I am trying to develop, I want to say that my early attitude toward the cause of war goes back to the days when I was a young man teaching a Bible class. We made a study of the causes of war, in particular those in connection with the first great war. I remember full well that in that discussion the name of Sir Basil ZaharofE came up. He was represented to have been a Greek private, but during the years 1914-18 he was in position to start selling service rifles to Greece and before the end of the war, during the course of five years, he was a multimillionaire selling battleships to the * opposing nations.
That is the kind of thing we have under private enterprise. He owned many newspapers throughout Europe which helped to build up the fear psychology, the same fear psychology we see being built up now. Certainly it is being built up on the part of private enterprise just the same as it was at that time. The only thing that happened to this Greek private was that he was given the name Sir Basil Zaharoff following the first great war.
Then coming to the second great war, we all know of instances that occurred, and I shall point out just one to carry it through. After the close of the war in 1945 the war tribunals were set up at Nuremberg and it was found that the I. G. Farben company had over 700 affiliated companies in 104 different countries, not less than seven of those associated companies being located in Canada. One can readily see the international cartelization and monopoly of today, and the extension of the profit system throughout the world. As far as I am concerned I do not care if there are brown shirts, black shirts or stuffed shirts; the time has come when people through their democracies have to get up and face people like my hon. friends, who are trying to guarantee to individuals in our economy that they can take the kind of profits they want when we are faced with an emergency in this country.
I think the time has come when we should consider the stewardship of the government in power. While I do not agree with the capitalist system, while I do not agree with the methods used to procure the necessities for defence, I do think we are all agreed that we need defence measures. However, I think we are paying many times over what we need to pay, simply because people like my hon. friends to my right are trying to safeguard the profits of the people who perhaps helped to put them here by means of campaign funds. I feel that we are missing


the boat, and that in the future this country may not be able to provide adequate defence measures.
So I say that unless the people of this country wake up, not to the issue raised by the hon. member for Greenwood but to the real issue of the stewardship of the resources of this country in peacetime and in wartime, we will not be able to bring to the people of the world a lasting peace.

Mr. Speaker, I think we have listened to the most mixed up and misled speech delivered for a long time in this house, or probably in any other house. I shall not take up too much of the time of the house, but I would like to indicate what is the attitude of the C.C.F. In this connection I should like to refer to what was said by the present leader of the C.C.F. on September 9, 1939, as follows:
4. Preservation of democracy at home: The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation protests against the encroachments on our civil liberties which the government has already introduced, and insists that democracy at home must be preserved unimpaired during the war.

We all
agree with that.

There it is. They want to preserve our civil liberties at home during wartime, but in a period which is not war they want to cast these liberties aside and hand over complete, arbitrary power to the government. That is an example of the consistency of the C.C.F. party and of the hon. member for Moose Mountain in particular.
So the hon. member for Moose Mountain and other misled members may understand the Conservative party's point of view-and I would have thought that by now they would have been able to get it through their heads-our attitude on this matter is that we believe powers of this kind are needed in wartime, are needed in case of emergency.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
You sit down. I shall listen to you later. I say that every member of this party who has risen to speak has said that we believe these powers are needed in emergencies; and when an emergency exists we shall be very glad to have the powers brought before parliament and will be glad to vote them in a democratic way. That, I believe, is the preservation of democratic rights, which your leader so clearly advocated when speaking on September 9, 1939, when a war was in progress.
The important thing in this whole controversy is what has gone on in the last four years to change the minister's mind in his

approach to this whole matter. Four years ago, on March 2, 1951, he said this, as reported on page 836 of Hansard:
It is proposed that the act would expire on July 31, 1956. There is no particular significance to this date other than to recognize that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature.
That was four years ago. At that time these powers were not required on a permanent basis. Today the leaders of countries all across the world tell us that tensions are less than they were even a year ago. World tensions are decreasing; yet today we are asked to make these sweeping powers permanent. What is the answer? The answer is, I believe, that this is simply a pattern which has been followed in the setting up of dictatorships for all time. First you have temporary powers requested to meet a specific emergency. Then a little while later these powers are quietly made permanent. That is the way dictatorships are created.
These powers certainly should be granted in any emergency, but they should not remain in the hands of this or any other government during a time when no emergency exists. I do not believe an emergency exists today. If one does, then bring these powers before parliament and explain the emergency. We shall be glad to grant the powers at any time an emergency exists, but not to grant them to this or any other government on a permanent basis. The granting of these powers on a permanent basis simply concentrates more and more power in the hands of a power-hungry government, or in the hands of any government which happens to be in office.
This kind of measure makes it possible for these powers to be used for other than military purposes. There is no question about that. If these powers, which cover the whole of the economy, are made permanent and become law, which I feel sure the Liberal government is going to do by means of its large majority, then I believe we ought to give this bill a new title. I think it should be called the "thermostat act," because it will enable this or any other government that happens to be in power to automatically apply the heat to any firm that shows a tendency to cool off in its desire to support the government.
That is a very bad thing. That kind of situation simply perpetuates whatever government happens to be in office. It is a tremendous potential power which a government can use if it wishes. To make it possible for any government to use that kind of power over industry is a very dangerous thing.
Defence Production Act
I strongly urge the Prime Minister, as every other member of this party does, to change this bill before it is passed; to take out the arbitrary power which is granted on a permanent basis, so these powers will be granted only in time of an emergency, by vote of parliament. If that were done I can assure you that this party, at any such time as an emergency exists, will be glad to cooperate and grant these powers to the government; -but we object to putting them on a permanent basis.
If the Prime Minister will do this he will be making a very important contribution toward democratic government in this country. I think it would be a fitting gesture for him and the Minister of Trade and Commerce to do this before they retire from active political life and leave this Liberal party of theirs to the chaos and confusion which will occur when the six hopefuls who will shortly be competing for the top spot-

If these powers are needed in an emergency we will be only too glad to grant them on an emergency basis, instead of putting them on a permanent basis. If an emergency is explained to parliament, we shall be glad to grant the necessary powers to the minister who is in charge of the department at that time. This arbitrary power is not needed on a permanent basis, either by the present minister or any other minister who may happen to be in charge of the defence production department in the future.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder how comfortable the right hon. Minister of Defence Production felt during that oration by the hon. member for Moose Mountain. It is certainly a peculiar part of the house from which to expect support for him. I believe he has been set up as the chief government representative of the principles of free enterprise. Yet in this house, except for two or three members of his own party, his sole support comes from those members to my left.
I am wondering at the same time whether perhaps he is not somewhat responsible for that situation. It seems to me that in the welter of propaganda we have heard, in the years even before the war, we have had built up for us a fantasy or a story of the one great man carrying the complete load in connection with this country's war effort. I do not believe he wanted it that way, but certainly as the press of this country ground out the story, and as the government propaganda

Defence Production Act machine was full at work, we appeared to forget the efforts of all the people which went into the struggle between 1939 and 1945.
In doing that I think we have left open the door to those who, like the hon. member for Moose Mountain, take every opportunity to point their finger at the people who in the long run saved this country for democracy. I might say to my friend the hon. member for Moose Mountain that he too would not be in this chamber and free to speak as he did today had it not been for the efforts of the people and the businesses who co-operated without exception in the most serious days this country ever faced.
However, I think I should again go over the reasons given by the minister in support of his argument that this legislation requires to be drafted in the form in which we have it now, and in no other way. The minister has referred to these specific points. First, he said that the work previously involved in purchasing for defence purposes was not nearly as complicated and difficult as it is today. Second, he stressed some features of defence production and referred to the tremendous obligation assumed by Canada for the mid-Canada early warning line. Third, he referred as well to plans under way for the development of a supersonic fighter plane made up of a supersonic airframe and a new supersonic engine. Fourth, though in a relative time of peace, he referred to the difficulty of maintaining our troops in Germany and in Canada. Fifth, combined with these problems which face this department there is no indication, according to the minister, of a reversion to ordinary times as contemplated in 1951, at the time of the original passing of this legislation. Sixth, in addition he suggested that there is ample opportunity to review the work of this department on its estimates, and I believe as well he mentioned the filing of the annual report pursuant to section 34 of the act. Seventh, as a clincher to these arguments he indicated that since 1939 some $17 or $18 billion have been spent by his various departments free from dishonesty, free from maladministration and free from the difficulties that frequently haunt defence purchasing.
Are these then sufficient reasons to prolong without restriction as to time in this department the powers contained in the present act? Frankly, these arguments sound more like those of a senior civil servant than of a minister of the crown. The senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), who appears to be the only official apologist for or defender of the department, has asked us

to be realistic in this situation. I think perhaps the most realistic approach to the situation was made by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) as he related his arguments to the ability of industry in Canada today to handle the requirements of the minister's department. Perhaps I might be permitted to pick up the threads of his argument and relate them directly to the case put forward by the minister and his parliamentary assistant.
First of all, it is true that the work of this department must be more complicated than it was in previous years or in the years before the war; but surely that work is no more complicated and no more exacting than is the work which must be performed by the officers of our large corporations in Canada today. They face the same problems, and they do so without the all-powerful provisions of an act such as this. There should be no particular difficulty in the government playing a strong hand without the benefit of an economic club.
The minister referred to the construction of the mid-Canada early warning line. I would assume that, to a great extent, the requirements for that line would be made up of electronic components and construction materials. I am sure the minister has read the Knox report and has read there of the problems facing the Canadian electronics industry in its fight to preserve full working time and full employment.
Perhaps the minister might refer to his associate the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Reinke) and ask him if he would have any difficulty in placing a contract with the Westinghouse company for items required for that particular job. The only thing I have heard from that company recently was an expression of deep regret that the impact of the requirements of the St. Lawrence seaway would only be of beneficial effect to that company by 1957, and then only in a limited way. Perhaps we might ask the same question of hon. members from the Toronto area, or perhaps of the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser). Is the electronics industry in Canada in a position to refuse, under any circumstances, to keep its workmen at their jobs?
I am sure also that we could refer to the various building material companies and find the same answer, and in connection with the supersonic fighting planes. Why are powers of this kind necessary to produce supersonic planes? I would think the minister is almost the sole customer of two of the largest plane manufacturers in this country. If he does not place the orders, they do not

work. Is there any necessity to have compulsion to develop a new plane, when those people are waiting and asking for the opportunity to produce in Canada those things which we need for national defence?
Then we have the argument with regard to maintaining troops in Canada and in Germany. I assume that among the chief requirements are supplies of clothing and of food. Perhaps the minister might refer to his associates, the hon. members for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) and Waterloo South (Mr. White), and ask them if any compulsion is necessary to obtain co-operation from the textile manufacturers and the producers of foodstuffs in those areas. I assume as well we can talk about the necessity for producing ships. I could refer to my colleague the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson), and ask him if there is any room in the shipyards in his riding to produce the necessary ships for our navy at this time.
No; when we become specific and enumerate the items one by one, there appears no place where we can fit in the necessity for compulsion so far as industry in Canada today is concerned. Then we talk about a reversion to ordinary times. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if we are not whistling in the dark. I wonder if these are not the ordinary times which we will face for the next 20 to 25 years, and if we do not have to have a new type of thinking, a new approach. When we talk about an emergency I think we have to divide it into two parts, an emergency from without and an emergency caused by economic conditions within our own country which prevent us from arming ourselves to meet the outside emergency.
There are no economic conditions in Canada today which place a disability on the minister's department to an extent which prevents the department from adequately preparing this country for defence. In reality every bit of evidence points to the fact that industry today first of all desires and in most cases requires-and I refer to shipbuilding and aircraft production-orders from the government to maintain full employment. How can we justify compulsion under circumstances of that kind?
If conditions are as I have indicated, then where can the minister find support for his argument that a continuation of these powers is necessary at this time? In the legal profession we like to be able to refer to precedent. Sometimes it may be a little embarrassing. I almost think perhaps the parliamentary assistant may wish he had not referred to precedent when he thinks about being on the immigration committee of the 50433-298i
Defence Production Act bar association. But generally speaking we look to precedent for support for our arguments.
If I may take a few minutes I should like to trace down through the years from 1939 the various powers that have been possessed by the minister in the various and numerous departments for which he has been responsible from time to time. The beginning of the history of these powers can be traced back to the department of munitions and supply act, statutes of Canada, 1939, chapter 3, which was assented to on September 13, 1939. This act was proclaimed on the 9th of April, 1940, and the wide powers contained therein were restricted to a period of three years. Section 16, subsection 1 of that act reads as follows:
Subject to the following provisions of this section, the foregoing provisions of this act shall continue in force for a period of three years beginning with the date of the passing of this act, and shall then expire . . .
That was 1939, and there was a restriction of powers at that time to three years. Then under an act to amend the department of munitions and supply act, statutes of Canada, 1940, chapter 31, the powers were again restricted to a period of three years under section 17, subsection 1, which reads:
Subject to the following provisions of this section, the foregoing provisions of this act shall continue in force for a period of three years beginning with the date of the passing of this act, and shall then expire . . .
That was 1940.

speechtext: Right in the midst of the war.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Then under an act to amend the department of munitions and supply act, statutes of Canada, 1943-44, chapter 8, the restriction contained under section 17 of the act of 1940 was deleted by section 9, subsection 1. This of course was still in one of the most difficult times this country ever faced, and is the only place I have found a record of freedom from a time limit on this type of power.
In the statutes of Canada, 1944-45, chapter 18, there are certain wide powers dealing with the department of reconstruction. Those powers were restricted under section 2(g), which reads as follows:
(g) "period of reconstruction" means the period beginning on April 1st, 1944, until the end of the session of parliament commencing in the fourth year following the cessation of hostilities between Canada and the German Reich and the empire of Japan.
In the statutes of Canada, 1945, chapter 16, the department of reconstruction and supply was created, and under section 6 the minister was given all the powers formerly vested in him as minister of munitions and supply and1 minister of reconstruction. I can only take-

Defence Production Act from that reference that the restriction in the original act dealing with reconstruction continued in the new act. By section 11 of the Department of Resources and Development Act, chapter 18, statutes of Canada, 1949, the department of reconstruction and supply came to an end. Section 11 reads:
The department of mines and resources act, the geology and mines act, the department of reconstruction act, 1944, and sections 1 to 8 of the department of reconstruction and supply act, 1945, are repealed.
That ended the powers contained in that act, although it left unaffected valid contracts which were entered into before the expiration of the act.
In the statutes of 1950, chapter 33, we find an act respecting defence supplies and projects. Section 9 (1) of this act repealed the department of munitions and supply act, which was chapter 3 of the statutes of 1939, second session. At this time we had no act containing powers on an indefinite basis.
In the statutes of 1950-51, chapter 6, we find an act respecting materials and services essential for the purposes of defence and national security. This act was to be administered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Section 10 of that act provided for its expiry on July 31, 1952. The section reads:
This act shall expire on the thirty-first day of July, nineteen hundred and fifty-two.
Here is the history since 1939 of dealings in provisions of this type, provisions which concentrate power in the hands of one man and contain serious restrictions on appeals to the courts and on the freedom of individuals. These are the precedents to which we must refer today. So far as I can determine they are the only ones, and it was only in the midst of the most devastating war in the history of this country that wide powers of this type were handed over without restriction as to time.
The senior member for Halifax indicated that we had used double talk in connection with this problem. I say there is no double talk. The recognition of someone as a great man is no indication that powers such as these should be granted to anyone under any circumstances short of the worst type of emergency that could face us. The senior member for Halifax has stated that we are opposing for the sake of opposition. When I listened to the minister read his statement in this house today I wondered whether, in all fairness, we could be accused of opposition for the sake of opposition.
I do not know whether this is some type of concession or some type of subterfuge. I do know this, that without the efforts of

Her Majesty's loyal opposition this statement would not have been made today. As I read it, I think it may even be a departure from the ordinary rules of this house. I am not sure that it has ever been done before. I am sure of one thing; it is an indication that the opposition still fills a very vital need in our parliamentary institutions.

speechtext:
Earlier this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) made a very apt quotation from Macaulay's "Horatius at the Bridge" which caused some merriment in the house. Nevertheless the quotation was very apt. At this moment I should like to give

another quotation from the classics, only a little farther in the past, namely from Aesop's Fables, which I think again illustrates the point in this bill that is before us.
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, the old story in Aesop's Fables about the toad who was the doctor and who practised medicine amongst the other animals of the jungle in Aesop's kingdom. Eventually one very ancient frog came up to the doctor and said, "Doctor, we are very glad to see you practising medicine in our kingdom, and you have been doing well on occasion and not so well on other occasions. We all think it would be a very good idea if you would cure your own warts first."
In Canada we have felt very proud of, and perhaps a little smug about, our tradition of parliamentary government. We look with a somewhat jaundiced eye on other countries that are not so fortunate as ourselves. We hold up our hands in holy horror, so to speak, at such iron curtain countries as Russia, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Rumania and so on. We even look at Spain askance at times, and at some of the Far Eastern countries who do not enjoy the democratic rights that we have. The idea that Canada has such a very fine system of parliamentary government is expounded at various international gatherings such as the United Nations. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has held up Canada as an example of a fine parliamentary government. The Prime Minister, who took a trip around the world, was also described as the head of a state which had possibly the finest parliamentary government with the exception of the mother of parliaments herself.
We in Canada sometimes look with a slight, snide sneer at our great next door neighbour. We say our system is really much better than theirs, and that is fine. I think that is correct. But I cannot help feeling that if this bill passes we shall be taking a step backward. In other words we shall be retrogressing in the system of parliamentary government we have built up after such long struggles from the time of Magna Carta right down to the present.
Some speakers have said that the people of Canada no longer care about principles, that they are just interested in what the government produces. I do not think that is so. I am not cynical in that regard; I feel the people do care.
With regard to this bill, many of my colleagues have pointed out the various objections to it. The hon. member for York West pointed out a number of things in the bill that he found objectionable. The only thing
Defence Production Act I personally find objectionable is the matter of having no time limit on the emergency powers. The objections on this ground have been well set out by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, but there are a few more points that I should like to deal with in the next few moments.
We are all agreed that there is a state of considerable emergency in the world, that certain powers to act quickly are necessary, and that the Minister of Defence Production must have those powers. There has been no suggestion by any hon. member on this side of the house that the Minister of Defence Production is not a very capable man. We are all agreed on that.

No, Mr. Speaker; I was thinking more specifically of the possibility of a socialist government.
It has been pointed out by some hon. members that it is not true that the Minister of Defence Production does not have to account to parliament under this act; that the estimates of that department come up for discussion and these matters can be discussed then, or on the amendment of an hon. member to the motion to go into supply. That is quite true, but it looks to me like trying to enter by the back door, in other words trying to do something indirectly that you cannot do directly.
It is a very great mistake to bring this thin edge of the wedge into the edifice of our parliamentary government. It is a bad principle and a step in the wrong direction. Once a principle is established there will be a further whittling away in the future.
The only thing the opposition has asked in this bill is that a time limit be put on it. Whether they wish to make the time limit 1958, 1957, 1956 or even 1959 is immaterial. A time limit should be placed on it. There is a possibility that the present cold war may cease and become-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

Thank you. The cold war may in fact cease to exist before too many years. In fact we are hopeful, and there are signs that at the moment an improvement is taking place and the act may not be so necessary. None of us has a crystal ball with which we can foresee the future. In the past some hon. members may have had one, but at the present time nobody has. Things may greatly improve in the world. Because of that I can see no reason why a time limit cannot be placed in this bill. If it is necessary to renew it at the end of that time I am sure hon. members will be glad to extend the powers. No reason has been given as to why there should not be a time limit placed on this bill.
This afternoon the senior hon. member for Halifax made some remarks. I listened to them very carefully. The only conclusion I could come to was that he misunderstood the arguments of the opposition, or he was hauling a hogshead of red herrings from the east coast into this house.
Before this matter comes to a vote I should like to hear some further reason given by some members of the government as to why no time limit can be placed on this bill. As has already been said, the principle itself is wrong. We have struggled for years to build up parliament as we know it today.

Our ancestors struggled for hundreds of years before us. If we pass this bill we shall be taking a step in the opposite direction. If it were possible to bring people like William Ewart Gladstone and George Brown to this country to expound the principles of Liberalism of the last century, I should like to know what they would say about the content of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, just as I started to speak I heard a remark, "small talk"; but it may develop into big talk. I was rather astounded at the statement by the Minister of Defence Production that he was irritated by the repetition of statements as to his ability and outstanding qualities. I would not doubt that for a moment, because he gets it continually from his own side. In fact other ministers get the same sort of repetitious statements as to how outstanding they are. Of course, as we have said on many occasions, I do not imagine they do not mean it. When you examine the amount of literature and propaganda that goes

out from the government side of the house, repeating time after time just how good the government are, and what wonders they have performed, I do not doubt for a moment that they do get fed up with some of their own malarkey, and they just cannot take more of it when it comes from this side of the house. Probably they do have a certain feeling of embarrassment at times over this continual repetition of their abilities.
The followers of the government have said they do not hear very many good speeches from this side of the house. Probably if some of the government followers were given an opportunity to say something we might hear a few good speeches. I do not doubt for a moment that there is hidden talent over there, and we would like to hear it. However, hon. gentlemen are generally silent when issues like this confront the country, and we hear very little from them.
When this bill was introduced it was said to be a simple bill. Sure it is simple; we all admit that. I suppose they thought they were talking to a lot of simpletons and they were going to get by with it, but now they find they are not.

We would be guilty of a failure to meet our responsibilities as members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition if we did not ferret out any dishonesty or evidence of dictatorship or autocratic power or arrogant conduct by the crown's officers, and reveal to the house and the people of Canada the manner in which the prerogatives of parliament are being filched. This is not a question of the minister's prestige, ability and all-round proven worth or political rectitude, as some hon. members have attempted to establish, but one of restoring and retaining parliament's right to determine, and preventing any derogation of its power.

Mr. Speaker, as it may be necessary at this time for me to talk a little longer than I usually do, I feel that I should perhaps apologize for being lengthy. I have always tried to follow the practice of being as brief as possible in my remarks. In fact one of my colleagues unflatteringly said that my speeches are short, sharp and shapeless. I do not know whether I should say that my speech now will be lengthy, light and loquacious. However, I want to preface my remarks with that comment.
Some person has unflatteringly termed this debate a filibuster. I could not help thinking back and wondering about the use of that word, which has had a good deal of prominence in the United States of America in the last few years. I do not know what the word "filibuster" means, because I did not have a chance to look it up, having had to prepare my brief notes hurriedly. Incidentally, may I say that debates of this sort give a person a chance to deliver the remarks he may make a little bit more from the heart and with more feeling than would be likely if he prepared his speech in guarded words.
In thinking of this term "filibuster" and the use of this word, one is reminded of the various filibusters that have taken place in the Senate of the United States. I recall reading of the senator in the United States who, in an attempt to filibuster some piece of legislation, read "Gone With the Wind" to the house. This filibuster gives one an idea of how this method can be used effectively to call public attention-as has been said- to these seemingly high-handed measures that are being proposed and which the government is attempting to put through the house in the closing days of the session, when we have important committee work and other duties to attend to.
In mentioning the United States, I was reminded of a recent honorary degree given by the University of New Brunswick to Senator Margaret Chase Smith, that distinguished woman senator from the state of Maine which borders Canada. Hon. Margaret

Defence Production Act Chase Smith was given the honour of delivering the encaenial address. At that time she delivered an oration that I know will be remembered by many in Fredericton. It was not my privilege to hear her, but I have read some of the remarks she made.
I should like to trace for a minute or two some of the pertinent issues she brought out with regard to the difficulty being experienced in the United States today, in the post-war world, to ensure that freedom of speech has been maintained. We are all familiar with the rise of McCarthyism within the last few years, and the pro-communist feeling that spread out in this great land to the south of us. In telling of this alarming condition that had been built up as a product of the war, Margaret Chase Smith referred to the American people-and I suppose she was thinking to some extent of those who were sitting in government-as mental mutes. Mr. Speaker, I say very seriously that I would not want to be considered a mental mute when an issue as important as this is before the house.
After referring to this difficulty that had cropped up in the United States and using the term "mental mutes", Margaret Chase Smith went on to say that fear and blind emotion had hit her fellow people, and that no more was independent thought available in the legislature and on the street where these issues should be originally considered. In completing her encaenial address she said she was quite pleased to report that they were able to combat that situation.
As we know, the rise of McCarthyism seems to have been stemmed for the time being, and in the United States there is a new feeling; under their new president, that great war leader Dwight Eisenhower, once more there seems to be the freedom of thought and the general freedom we all fought so hard to maintain in these last two great wars.
In regard to this piece of legislation which has the controversial section and which asks for extraordinary powers, I feel there are two important issues at stake, and it is rather difficult to separate them one from the other. I have loosely termed these two criticisms as bureaucracy and socialism. As you will note right off the bat, as the phrase goes, they are almost interchangeable. I will not attempt to separate my thoughts with respect to each, but I should like to deal first with this matter of bureaucracy, which has been covered more ably than I can do by the more brilliant lawyers of this party who appreciate the rule of law and what it means.
When the hon. member for Prince Albert makes his impassioned pleas in behalf of a bill of rights and the rule of law, I have


noticed how he is scorned and gibed at by those on the opposite side of the house. Even the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has once or twice referred to those strong pleas as the shades of the star chamber. Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, star chamber or not, I think we all realize or should realize 

those of the legal profession perhaps more than the rest of us-the great principles that are involved in this rule of law, in this delegated legislation, and this term I have used when I refer to bureaucracy.
In coming down here late this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I happened to pick up a list of the members of the House of Commons. In running through it quickly I was wondering just how many of the lawyers on the opposite side of the house-those who should appreciate to the fullest extent the principles that are involved in this legislation-had taken this matter into consideration. I was wondering how much thought they have given to it, and the extraordinary powers that are sought. First of all I come to New Brunswick and the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy), a young lawyer starting out in his profession. I wonder how much consideration he has given to this legislation. I go down the list and in the province of Ontario I see the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth). I believe he is a lawyer. I wonder what he feels about this legislation.
