The section of the article that is obviously pertinent here is entitled, "Functions of Government and the Administration of the Law". Of course the article refers particularly to politics and the law rather than to the actual judges themselves. In the article Mr. Friedmann mentions the transformation of the social pattern that has come about in the post-war world when it is necessary to have some sort of semi-mobilization of our forces even after passing through an emergency which was such a trial to the whole of western society. He goes on to say at page 823:
Such a transformation of society cannot but have a profound-though still largely unnoticed-effect on legal concepts and relations.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the point I am trying to make. I suggest that in the post-war world there has been a transformation of our society profound in its effect, but which as yet has not been too greatly felt and has gone unnoticed. Our lawyers, those watchdogs of our rights and the principles of common law, should feel that there is a responsibility and onus upon them to consider these matters, speak up and have their say. That is one article which was commended to me, and it is of fairly recent date. I did not search for articles, Mr. Speaker, but in every issue of the Canadian Bar Review there is comment on the gradual growth of administrative law, and reference to the cases and various decisions.
I turn now to another article found in volume 30, 1952, which deals very extensively with the question of inherent executive power and the steel seizure case, a landmark in American constitutional law. The reference of course is to the situation that arose when, on April 8, 1952, President Truman found it necessary to invoke certain powers and take over the steel industry.
There is one other article in the same volume that has come to my attention. It is found on page 791 and is entitled, "The War Power of the Dominion". The article begins with the British North America Act and traces the development of the various powers that have arisen. It points out that the only particular reference to war in any way in the British North America Act is of course, as we know, in section 92, which gives the residual power to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada. Of course at that time the legislators did not envisage modern warfare and its related problems. The article deals with the cases, going back to our early history, and the conclusion is reached that there is an inherent danger, a danger that is not fully appreciated by all concerned.

The hon. member for Eglinton referred briefly in his remarks to a book which is very widely read nowadays, entitled "The Passing of Parliament" by Professor G. W. Keeton. Professor Keeton deals with the passing of parliament and the growth of delegated legislation in a most commendable way. He refers to the dangers I have mentioned and to the fact that there are two main criticisms today of our modern parliaments.
These criticisms are just as valid in England, where the opposition is almost equal in numbers to the government party. It is true that this balance has been upset to some extent in recent days. I think it was on May 26 that we received the good news. The issue in Great Britain is still the same, even when the opposition is nearly equal in numbers to that of the government. It is just as dangerous as in Canada where the opposition is, I think we can modestly say, effective even though its numbers are few. It is for that reason we have considerable difficulty in focusing the attention of the country on this issue. It is for that reason we have to strain various methods in order to prove the principle of the supremacy of parliament, and bring out these issues. It is the duty of Her Majesty's loyal opposition to do that job.
This article to which I have referred is entitled "The Passing of Parliament," and I cannot help but think back to the various articles in the newspapers that seem to have been given a bit of prominence in the last year or two. I am not going to read this next article, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to say it is a very good one. It is written by Frank Flaherty and it is entitled "Public Discussion called Press Freedom Safeguard". Mr. Flaherty in this commendable article of recent date discusses the bill of rights and the great fight that has been waged by the hon. member for Prince Albert in that respect. He refers to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and others who have spoken in this regard. He mentions the preservation of freedoms of all kinds.
He refers to the freedom of the press. We all know that the freedom of the press can only be implemented to its fullest extent when these issues are brought out in the only effective way that can be done, by such discussions as these in parliament when hon. members do not read these prepared speeches. We are all guilty of that to some extent, but we feel that perhaps hon. members opposite are a little guiltier. This is an opportunity that comes up every now and then. It gives hon. members a chance


to speak without too much preparation, to give their own thoughts and feelings about conditions in this world today.
In connection with this same subject, I might say that if Canada's only desire was to wage war efficiently we could solve many of our problems for a time. At such a time even a democracy completely abandons much of the freedom upon which it ordinarily sets such store:	All is subordinated to military
necessity, but the chickens come home to roost at last as democracies and dictatorships alike learned after the last war. This is a lesson we have learned to our sorrow. All I hope to state here is that a democracy, soundly based upon free opinion and the judgment of responsible people, in the long-run weathers the storm better than those governments which are least responsible to public opinion.
I have dealt as effectively as possible with the first step I mentioned, and which I placed under the heading of bureaucracy. If I may just review what I said in that regard, I traced the rule of law and mentioned the passing of parliament; all that sort of thing. There was one other article which commended itself to me most highly, and I should like to give credit in that regard. It referred to this same issue, and with this I shall leave it, Mr. Speaker. It referred to "The Passing of Parliament" by Keeton, and appeared in the Ottawa Journal of March 3, 1954. It was written by James McCook, who has more than an ordinary interest in these various issues that come up and the principles that are behind our form of government.
Mr. McCook went on to ask whether parliament had been supplanted, and he suggested that government by the people is the least perfect. He referred to the controls that had been built up in England by this delegated legislation, and he likened it somewhat to the similar legislation which is showing itself in a very ugly way in this fair dominion of ours. Let me paraphrase him, Mr. Speaker. He said the fact that parliament should impose its will on an individual is nothing new, but the tendency is for parliament to give arbitrary powers to boards and to by-pass the courts where the citizen has been accustomed to seek justice. In most departments of government today no minister could possibly keep track of all that is happening. He has to depend more and more on the civil service, which in consequence has great power. Then the article continues:
He says that if a member says a word about the civil service the minister of the department concerned immediately declares, "I am responsible; attack me".
How strange it is that the responsible ministers who have placed this legislation

I suggest that in this legislation there is the means of maintaining a socialist welfare system, of dislocating capitalism and at the same time furthering the ends of that party.

The issues are drawn; it is one of the most clear-cut positions that could possibly be maintained. It is amazing, the inconsistency shown by that party. It was slow to take its part, rightly or wrongly, in the war in 1939; it had reservations about West Germany, and yet here where extraordinary powers are being given to one man the socialists want to climb aboard and support the proposal. I suggest that they are doing this because they see here something that can be used to further their own ends.
Our position is definite and clear in connection with the powers that may be hidden in various pieces of legislation. We have suggested that a body similar to the Hoover commission be set up. There was an investigation in Great Britain into cabinet power, and we feel that something should be done here. It is interesting to note that once such power is obtained by a government in various small ways they never wish to give it up. I would refer more specifically to the identity cards which were instituted during the war in the allied countries. They were necessary for registration purposes, but they have been continued in some form in those places. There is an example of the danger I see. Once power is given it is never taken away.
I was interested in reading in the papers today reference to the granting of a guaranteed annual wage in the United States. General Motors were not as concerned about this plan as was Ford, because they knew that the cost of the guaranteed annual wage could be added to their war contracts. I suggest that perhaps that is another reason for it.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I shall simply restate my position and say that in my opinion the arbitrary powers asked for in this legislation show two very worrisome dangers. They deal with our fundamental principles of government. I have placed them under two headings. Perhaps they are a little hard to distinguish. I mentioned the bureaucracy that is present. I referred to the derogation of the rule of law. I called on the reputable lawyers in this house. I stated what the younger lawyers of my own age thought of it, though they may be immature. speechtext:
Indeed I am. We have some quotations in which the socialist party may be interested, from their own remarks of four years ago. Before we come to that, it may be desirable to state in as simple terms as possible the issue we have before us. That is, that all parties in the house today are prepared to see the Department of Defence Production placed upon a permanent basis in order that the minister may have the necessary legislative authority for the recruitment of officials and the making of plans for the procurement of defence requirements. The official opposition are not prepared to see the act continued without any limitation upon the arbitrary controls placed in the hands of the minister and the governor in council.
We are stating here no new proposition. I see that the Prime Minister is in sudden unity with the Minister of Defence Production in the house. I remind the Prime Minister that four years ago, when the Defence Production Act was introduced on his motion, as this extending bill was introduced on his motion, a limitation was written into the duration of the act. That has had two effects, namely that the authority of the department itself would expire on July 31, 1956, unless otherwise extended; and, more important,
Defence Production Act that the sweeping, arbitrary powers given the governor in council and the minister would also expire on that date.
At that time the Prime Minister felt that was a proper limit to write into the bill. We have heard no word whatsoever, since this present motion was introduced, as to why it is no longer proper to write in a time limit on those arbitrary powers. The house, I know, awaits with interest-indeed, I might almost say with anxiety-an explanation from the Prime Minister as to why in 1955 it should not be necessary or desirable to have the same limitation.
Of course, the Prime Minister has been in office for four years longer now than when the bill was first introduced. So perhaps he, along with the rest of his colleagues, has fallen under the magic spell of the Minister of Defence Production. This seems to indicate that so far as those on the other side are concerned, at any rate, arbitrary powers are their own justification; and that whereas four years ago the house was entitled to an explanation as to their necessity and as to a time limit in the bill so the house might have an opportunity to review the exercise of those powers, in 1955, four years later, no such safeguards or parliamentary jurisdiction or supremacy are necessary.
Of course we should also bear in mind that we are discussing this measure tonight under the circumstance that some three months ago, when the resolution was first introduced, the Prime Minister himself indicated that the government would be prepared to consider what was after all a reasonable request, namely that they should try to write into the act some time limit with regard to the duration of these arbitrary powers. During the four days this debate has been in progress-today and Thursday, Wednesday and Tuesday of last week-we have had no explanation from the right hon. gentleman as to why he came to the decision that it would not be possible to write such a limitation into the act.
Why is it that what was a reasonable suggestion in March of this year we should now be asked to regard as an unreasonable suggestion? Why is it that tonight all my hon. friends of the socialist party are clamouring as loudly as my hon. friends of the Liberal party to have the question voted on and to get it through? They say we should have the vote; we do not need the arguments. What reason is there that now, in June, the house should be denied an explanation? Why is it that what was reasonable three months ago is no longer reasonable? The only conclusion one can draw is that the Minister of Defence Production has once again had

Defence Production Act his undisputed way with the cabinet. What are we left to conclude are the reasons of the government as to why this measure should carry without a time limit on the exercise of these arbitrary powers?
There have been remarkably few speakers on the government side. There has been the Minister of Defence Production himself, to whose speech I shall have occasion to make reference later, and there has been his parliamentary assistant, the senior member for Halifax. I say this with regret, but it appears to me that to such straits are the government reduced that the best argument they can make in favour of the bill is a complete distortion of the statements of hon. members on this side.
I have been informed of the arguments used by the hon. senior member for Halifax this morning. I must say that he read into the statements of members on this side of the house, such as that of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery), that which just is not there. Of course, as I say, the hon. member may be hard put to it to find an argument, but I should hope that he can find something better than the complete distortion of what is said by those on this side of the house.
He accused the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton of having said-and I think his words were "having said in ringing tones"- that we will do anything the Minister of Defence Production asks. If I recall correctly what the hon. gentleman said, he repeated the statement; he repeated that the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton said that we on this side of the house would do anything the minister asked.
All I can say is that I have had the opportunity of reading in detail the speech of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, and I have asked my colleagues to read it. Between us we have read it some three or four times. Nowhere in that speech, and nowhere in the statements of anyone on this side of the house, is there such an absurd, inconsistent, meaningless and ridiculous statement that we have made such an abdication of our responsibilities as members of parliament that we will do anything the minister asks.
What we did say was this, and we say it again. We are prepared to support the proposal to place the Department of Defence Production on a permanent basis so long as the need for that department can be justified; but we are not prepared to consent to the continuation, without limit, of wartime powers-indeed, powers that go far beyond some of those that were taken in wartime- in time of peace to the complete denial of the

principle of the supremacy of parliament, the principle of responsible government and the principle of the rule of law.
In the course of this debate we have heard one statement and a number of irrelevant interruptions from the Minister of Defence Production. I should have said that we have heard two statements from the Minister of Defence Production in which he was or attempted to be somewhat placatory and to reassure us on this side of the house; these statements were to the effect that the minister did not mean to take away from parliament any rights that belonged to it, but that all he was asking for were powers that he would exercise only in the national interest.
The fact remains, however, that the minister asks for arbitrary powers for an unlimited period of time. The minister is there in his place. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is in his place beside him. If I am incorrect in my statement that what is asked for here is the continuation of arbitrary powers for an unlimited period of time, I should be glad to be corrected. In the absence of any correction I take it that my statement represents the facts with which this house is confronted.
I should like to refer the house-and I hope the words may be read by a wider audience than this house, Mr. Speaker, or even yourself-to statements which I find contained in a pamphlet entitled "The Rule of Law". The pamphlet is headed "A Study by the Inns of Court Conservative and Unionist Society". It is published on the authority of the Conservative political centre in the United Kingdom. I make reference to the auspices under which this pamphlet is published because, as I shall have occasion to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house later, if there is one thing that characterizes those of conservative mind throughout the world- here in Canada, as in the United Kingdom and in all the other commonwealth countries -and differentiates them so completely from those who now follow what they call Liberal tenets or socialist tenets, it is our dedication to the principles of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law.
In the foreword to this pamphlet I find words that might well commend themselves to and I think should command the attention -though I doubt whether they will-of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production. Those- words are as follows:
Those who give and those who receive arbitrary power are alike criminal and there is no man but is bound to resist it to the best of his power, whenever it shall show its face in the world. It is a crime to bear it when it can be rationally shaken off . . . Law and arbitrary power are in dreadful enmity.

These are the words of a great Conservative, and they are as true today as they were when they were uttered. As I say, they are the words of a great Conservative; I refer to Edmund Burke.
What are we faced with here? We are faced with a demand or ultimatum to parliament that we continue in the hands of the governor in council and of the Minister of Defence Production arbitrary power for an unlimited time, the necessity for which and the duration of which there has been no shadow of justification shown. So we rest our case on the principle enunciated by Burke, namely that it is a crime to bear such arbitrary power when it can be rationally shaken off-as it can be now-and that law and arbitrary power are in dreadful enmity.
Then just in case you, Mr. Speaker, or my colleagues in this house or the people of the country should wonder whether I am not overstating the case when I say the Minister of Defence Production has laid down an ultimatum not only to us in the house but to his colleagues in the cabinet, I refer you to words which he used when the act, the continuation of which is now sought, was being discussed in this house on March 8, 1951. Then as you will recall for four or five days we discussed the various proposals of that bill in committee. Admitting as we do now the necessity for a defence production act, but seeking on every occasion to bring about a realistic limitation of these arbitrary powers, we suggested amendments to a number of sections which would have the effect of preserving the rights of the Canadian people and the rights of this parliament.

Defence Production Act Four years ago, when the bill to bring into being the defence production department was before the house, we objected to the broad and sweeping powers that were given to the minister, to the governor in council, to the controllers and investigators who could be appointed by the minister and who were not even to be held responsible in courts of law for their acts, provided they were done after they had been appointed. The minister objected. He said, "We cannot leave these things to the courts of law". Why, heavens above, he said, the courts of law take time to consider the rights of the citizen and whether or not the rights of the citizen have been trammelled and trampled upon. He said "We are not prepared to allow that time. Leave it to us, the government, and we will ensure that the liberties and rights of citizens are protected".
The Conservative party in the United Kingdom, having surveyed these and similar arguments, came to this conclusion:
This is not the first time in our history that problems of law and liberty have arisen. In the 17th century, too. claims were put forward that the executive could be trusted to act to the best advantage of the country as a whole; that the sec. tional interests represented in parliament should be kept to their proper sphere, which was discussion rather than interference with the exercise of prerogative powers; that the rigidity of courts of law, with their emphasis on individual rights, hindered efficient administration; that executive processes should be justiciable, if at all, by tribunals more flexible, less bound by precedent, more cognizant of administrative needs than the traditional courts.
Then they go on to say:
Freedom from arbitrary arrest, freedom of discussion, the principle that no one should be compelled to pay fines or taxes or to suffer loss of property except in accordance with an act of parliament interpreted in independent courts of law-
All these principles are denied by the minister, denied by the legislation we have before us tonight.
these great bulwarks of our civil liberty were firmly established.
It is therefore a denial of the constitution when these great bulwarks of liberty are set aside, as they would be under this bill. Then too, Mr. Speaker, we had the Minister of Defence Production denying in the house last Tuesday that to pass this bill, and thus to continue for an indefinite term the arbitrary powers with which he and the government are vested, would be an abrogation of parliamentary supremacy. Once again, in case it should be hard to believe, as indeed I find it hard to believe in the light of some of the provisions of the act which are to be continued for an indefinite period, I should like to read what the minister said as reported 

at page 4510 of Hansard for Tuesday, June 7. At that time the minister said:
At the resolution stage the Leader of the Opposition implied that in asking for the continuation of the Defence Production Act the government is getting away from the traditional methods of parliamentary procedure and parliamentary responsibility, and that there is a denial of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. I must admit that I am only a layman in this field-
That reminds me a little of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) who says he is only a poor, uneducated man, but he is not uneducated in the exercise of arbitrary power. The Minister of Defence Production continued:
X must admit that I am only a layman in this field, but it seems to me that this is not the case. Under our present parliamentary procedures the house has an opportunity to review the responsibilities and functions of each department at least once a year, when the estimates are being considered. Traditionally this is the way in which legislation can be examined critically, the way in which it can be determined whether or not it meets the needs and conditions of the times.
The minister was suggesting to us that by a review of his departmental estimates when they came before us we could achieve the result we desire. We do not know when that may be. Perhaps he will follow the lead of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), who when he was minister of citizenship and immigration found there were certain controversial matters in his department and held off his estimates deliberately until the day scheduled for the closing of the session. The governor general had been summoned to come and close parliament, but the minister said, "You will have an opportunity for a full and adequate discussion of everything my department does."
I find no indication that the Minister of Defence Production has shown any interest in having his estimates brought on early in this session. That is the cold comfort with which this house is to be left as a compensation for passing this legislation, with its continuation for an unlimited term of these sweeping and arbitrary powers. I point out also that in the department there are but seven items covering $26 million; just seven items in the minister's whole department, of which one is statutory so parliament will never have an opportunity to debate it.
I ask you, sir, could anything be more ridiculous, could anything be more indicative of the effrontery, the buffoonery with which parliament is confronted, than to be asked to take that as a guarantee we will have the opportunity to make a thorough review of the exercise of these arbitrary powers? minister. I have heard those words echoed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of the C.C.F. party, a gentleman whom I normally find to be somewhat impressed with the importance of maintaining the supremacy of parliament. All my hon. friends of the socialist party have fallen victim to the same line of reasoning and are clamouring and banging their desks to get the bill through, knowing perfectly well that in the examination of the estimates there is afforded to the house a very imperfect and slight opportunity for a real review of what goes on behind the closed doors of the governor in council, the cabinet, and the exercise of ministerial discretion and passage of ministerial decrees. To talk about reviewing these things done in secret in the committee of supply is but a travesty of the democratic process.
I have here again the words of the pamphlet to which I have referred, "Rule of Law", a study carried out by a committee comprising a large number of members of parliament in the United Kingdom, members who had had experience both in opposition and in government at the time the pamphlet was written. Parliament has neither the time nor the knowledge to supervise the minister and call him to account for his administrative decisions. Take the case where the minister appoints an inspector to hold a public inquiry and to report to him.

The report is not made public, nor does any outsider know what facts or arguments may be put forward to the minister after the inquiry has closed. Furthermore, the minister often fails to state, or state with sufficient fulness-
How often have we been confronted with that situation here in committee of supply?
-on what facts or reasons his ultimate decision is based. Where, then, is the material on which parliament can exercise control to prevent injustice? Even where a miscarriage comes to light, it is generally too late for redress.

Defence Production Act that in our own special committee on estimates there were about 10 votes when that committee asked for information or the production of documents or called for witnesses. One recognizes that parliament has every right to deal with policy, and no one wishes to stifle discussions on policy, but on the detailed day-to-day implementation of policy it can really become very burdensome and the machine could be entirely clogged if every single decision were subject to the possibility of public debate in this house or another place.
That is the end of the quotation from Lord Silkin, a socialist minister of town and country planning. The authors of the pamphlet continue:
These words are no more than a realistic appraisal of the facts of political and administrative life. They make it perfectly clear, if further testimony were needed, that parliamentary control provides no effective safeguard to the citizen aggrieved by official injustice.
Well, sir, that is the situation which confronts us tonight. The government is asking parliament to approve this bill which continues without limitation the arbitrary powers including the power of administrative decision, the power to regulate the economy, to dispossess a citizen of his property by secret

Defence Production Act order in council without recourse to the courts of law. Parliament is asked to set the stamp of its approval upon the principle enunciated by Lord Silkin, with the inevitable results stated in this pamphlet that the citizen aggrieved by official injustice would have no effective recourse whatsoever. I say to you, sir, that we of the Conservative party, holding true as we do to the principle of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law, will have no part in such legislation.
As I said earlier, it is interesting to see how the words of the Prime Minister, enunciated on an earlier occasion, have come home to roost. I recall that when he was appealing to the people of Canada for support in an election he said to those who might otherwise have voted for the socialists, "Do not vote for them; vote for us because they are only Liberals at heart. They just want to introduce the socialist state a little sooner than we will introduce it". Here we have the complete circuit, and the Prime Minister's words are brought home in a real, forceful manner. Here we have the Prime Minister introducing a bill but, for some reason which I am unable to understand, not having the respect for parliament to speak to the motion which introduces this dictatorial step; and he has the complete support of my friends of the socialist party.

After all, we are constantly reminded of the place of the members of the press under our parliamentary system. They are the fourth estate; they are part of our parliamentary system, and naturally we pay great attention to those newspapers which with their freedom of speech are able to discuss public affairs and present opinions from an objective point of view. The act in the United Kingdom similar to this one is the ministry of supply act, 1939, as amended by the supplies and services act, which was passed in 1945 and which has had certain minor amendments since then. That act is known as the Supplies and Services (Transitional Powers) Act, 1945. It is an act of ten sections which confers powers to deal with supplies and services. It contains few of the broad, unlimited powers contained in our act. There is no similarity whatever.
I do not believe that an act such as ours would be supported by the socialists in Westminster, after the educational period they had in government.
